cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The acute stress scenario embedded in the 30-day LCR period includes a partial loss of wholesale funding, a complete loss of retail deposits, reduced haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.
cards.explanation: The LCR stress scenario has a partial loss of deposits (they are comparatively sticky) and a complete loss of wholesale funding, and haircuts on secured funding increase rather than fall.
cards.originalText: A partial loss of wholesale funding, a complete loss of retail deposits, reduced haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The acute stress scenario embedded in the 30-day LCR period includes a partial loss of deposits, a complete loss of wholesale funding, increased haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.
cards.explanation: Alongside a three-notch downgrade, the LCR scenario assumes a partial loss of deposits, a complete loss of wholesale funding, increased haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.
cards.originalText: A partial loss of deposits, a complete loss of wholesale funding, increased haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The acute stress scenario embedded in the 30-day LCR period includes a complete loss of deposits, a partial loss of wholesale funding, increased haircuts on secured funding, and cancellation of undrawn lines of credit.
cards.explanation: Deposits suffer a partial loss and wholesale funding a complete loss, and customers draw down their lines of credit; cancellation would reduce outflows, which is the wrong direction for a stress scenario.
cards.originalText: A complete loss of deposits, a partial loss of wholesale funding, increased haircuts on secured funding, and cancellation of undrawn lines of credit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The acute stress scenario embedded in the 30-day LCR period includes a partial loss of deposits, a complete loss of wholesale funding, reduced haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.
cards.explanation: Haircuts on secured funding increase in the LCR stress scenario, since stress reduces the cash raised per unit of collateral.
cards.originalText: A partial loss of deposits, a complete loss of wholesale funding, reduced haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The liquidity coverage ratio's numerator includes regulatory capital, because regulatory capital is a component of high-quality liquid assets.
cards.explanation: Regulatory capital is not an asset and is not part of HQLA. It appears in the numerator of the net stable funding ratio, as a category of available stable funding.
cards.originalText: The liquidity coverage ratio, because regulatory capital is a component of high-quality liquid assets.
cards.correction: The net stable funding ratio's numerator includes regulatory capital, because regulatory capital is a component of available stable funding.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The net stable funding ratio's numerator includes regulatory capital, because regulatory capital is a component of available stable funding.
cards.explanation: Regulatory capital is not an asset and is not part of HQLA. It appears in the numerator of the net stable funding ratio, as a category of available stable funding.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The net stable funding ratio's numerator includes regulatory capital, because available stable funding is computed by applying available stable funding factors to each category of funding, including capital.
cards.explanation: The NSFR numerator (available stable funding) multiplies each funding category, including capital at a 100% ASF factor, by its ASF factor. The LCR numerator is a stock of liquid assets and excludes capital.
cards.originalText: The net stable funding ratio, because available stable funding is computed by applying available stable funding factors to each category of funding, including capital.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: A one-year retail term deposit receives a lower available stable funding factor than short-term wholesale funding obtained from another financial institution, because retail depositors are more numerous and therefore harder to monitor.
cards.explanation: Retail term deposits are among the most stable funding a bank has and receive a higher ASF factor than short-term wholesale funding from other financial institutions, which is the least stable category.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Cash and central bank reserves receive a required stable funding factor at the low end of the scale while long-dated performing loans receive a factor at the high end, because the latter must be funded on a durable basis.
cards.explanation: Cash requires almost no durable funding behind it, so its RSF factor is at the bottom of the scale, while long-dated performing loans must be funded for their whole life and sit near the top.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Regulatory capital is assigned a required stable funding factor of 100%, reflecting the permanence of the funding it supplies to the balance sheet.
cards.explanation: Capital is a funding source and belongs in available stable funding, the NSFR numerator, where it is weighted by an ASF factor rather than a required stable funding factor.
cards.correction: Regulatory capital is assigned an available stable funding factor of 100%, reflecting the permanence of the funding it supplies to the balance sheet.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Regulatory capital is assigned an available stable funding factor of 100%, reflecting the permanence of the funding it supplies to the balance sheet.
cards.explanation: Capital is a funding source and belongs in available stable funding, the NSFR numerator, where it is weighted by an ASF factor rather than a required stable funding factor.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: The available stable funding factor applied to a liability rises as its remaining maturity shortens, since short-dated funding can be rolled over more frequently and is therefore continuously renewed.
cards.explanation: The ASF factor falls as remaining maturity shortens. Frequent rollover is a vulnerability, since each rollover is a point at which funding can be withdrawn.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, the board of directors should develop the liquidity risk management strategy, policies and practices, and senior management should review and approve them at least annually.
cards.explanation: Senior management develops the liquidity risk strategy, policies and practices; the board reviews and approves them at least annually (Principle 3).
cards.originalText: The board of directors should develop the liquidity risk management strategy, policies and practices, and senior management should review and approve them at least annually.
cards.correction: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, senior management should develop the liquidity risk management strategy, policies and practices, and the board of directors should review and approve them at least annually.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, senior management should develop the liquidity risk management strategy, policies and practices, and the board of directors should review and approve them at least annually.
cards.explanation: Senior management develops the liquidity risk strategy, policies and practices; the board reviews and approves them at least annually (Principle 3).

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, liquidity costs, benefits and risks should be incorporated into internal pricing, performance measurement and new product approval for all significant business activities, both on and off balance sheet.
cards.explanation: This is Principle 4, which explicitly extends to off-balance-sheet activities.
cards.originalText: Liquidity costs, benefits and risks should be incorporated into internal pricing, performance measurement and new product approval for all significant business activities, both on and off balance sheet.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, supervisors should assess a bank's liquidity risk management framework but should not intervene in its liquidity position, which remains the sole responsibility of the bank.
cards.explanation: Principle 16 states that supervisors should intervene to require effective and timely remedial action where a bank is deficient.
cards.originalText: Supervisors should assess a bank's liquidity risk management framework but should not intervene in its liquidity position, which remains the sole responsibility of the bank.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, a bank should maintain a cushion of high-quality liquid assets, which may be encumbered provided they are held at the parent entity.
cards.explanation: Principle 12 requires the liquidity cushion to be unencumbered, with no legal, regulatory or operational impediment to its use.
cards.originalText: A bank should maintain a cushion of high-quality liquid assets, which may be encumbered provided they are held at the parent entity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, the contingency funding plan is the responsibility of the bank's supervisor, who sets out the strategies for addressing liquidity shortfalls in emergency situations and tests them regularly.
cards.explanation: Principle 11 places the contingency funding plan with the bank itself, including the obligation to test and update it. Supervisors assess the framework rather than author the plan.
cards.originalText: The contingency funding plan is the responsibility of the bank's supervisor, who sets out the strategies for addressing liquidity shortfalls in emergency situations and tests them regularly.
cards.correction: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, the contingency funding plan is the responsibility of the bank itself, which sets out the strategies for addressing liquidity shortfalls in emergency situations and tests them regularly.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, the contingency funding plan is the responsibility of the bank itself, which sets out the strategies for addressing liquidity shortfalls in emergency situations and tests them regularly.
cards.explanation: Principle 11 places the contingency funding plan with the bank itself, including the obligation to test and update it. Supervisors assess the framework rather than author the plan.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, a bank should conduct stress tests on a regular basis for a variety of short-term and protracted, institution-specific and market-wide scenarios, and should use the outcomes to adjust its liquidity risk management strategies, policies and positions.
cards.explanation: This is Principle 10: regular stress tests across a range of scenarios, with results fed back into strategy, policies and positions.
cards.originalText: A bank should conduct stress tests on a regular basis for a variety of short-term and protracted, institution-specific and market-wide scenarios, and should use the outcomes to adjust its liquidity risk management strategies, policies and positions.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, supervisors should communicate with other supervisors and public authorities within national borders only, since cross-border information sharing is properly the responsibility of the banks themselves.
cards.explanation: Principle 17 requires supervisors to communicate with other supervisors and public authorities both within and across national borders.
cards.originalText: Supervisors should communicate with other supervisors and public authorities within national borders only, since cross-border information sharing is properly the responsibility of the banks themselves.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
cards.statement: Under the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, a bank's funding strategy should concentrate on a small number of proven funding sources, since diversification across tenors dilutes relationships with funds providers and reduces fund-raising capacity.
cards.explanation: Principle 7 requires effective diversification in both the sources and the tenor of funding, alongside strong relationships with funds providers. Concentration is the vulnerability the principle exists to prevent.
cards.originalText: A bank's funding strategy should concentrate on a small number of proven funding sources, since diversification across tenors dilutes relationships with funds providers and reduces fund-raising capacity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A liquidity black hole arises when a price decline attracts contrarian buyers, so that prices revert quickly to fundamental value and the market clears.
cards.explanation: A liquidity black hole is defined by the absence of stabilising buyers: a price decline causes more participants to want to sell, driving prices well below where they eventually settle.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A uniform regulatory environment can contribute to liquidity black holes, because banks holding similar positions respond identically when volatilities and correlations rise, all seeking to reduce exposure at the same time.
cards.explanation: When volatilities and correlations rise, VaR-based capital requirements rise for all banks at once, and banks with similar positions all cut exposure at the same time, creating a one-sided market.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Life insurance companies and pension funds should be subject to the same market risk capital rules as banks, so that no type of institution gains a competitive advantage.
cards.explanation: They should not: longer-horizon institutions such as insurers and pension funds should not be penalised for holding illiquid assets or forced to rebalance when volatilities spike.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: The Basel Committee addressed procyclicality in credit risk capital by requiring probability of default estimates to reflect current point-in-time conditions.
cards.explanation: To reduce procyclicality the Basel Committee required through-the-cycle average probabilities of default rather than point-in-time estimates.
cards.correction: The Basel Committee addressed procyclicality in credit risk capital by requiring probability of default estimates to reflect through-the-cycle average conditions.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: The Basel Committee addressed procyclicality in credit risk capital by requiring probability of default estimates to reflect through-the-cycle average conditions.
cards.explanation: To reduce procyclicality the Basel Committee required through-the-cycle average probabilities of default rather than point-in-time estimates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Widespread use of stop-loss rules contributes to a stable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Stop-loss rules are a permanent source of positive feedback trading: automatic sales triggered when prices fall reinforce the decline and drain liquidity.
cards.originalText: Widespread use of stop-loss rules by participants on the platform.
cards.correction: Widespread use of stop-loss rules contributes to an unstable market with respect to liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Widespread use of stop-loss rules contributes to an unstable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Stop-loss rules are a permanent source of positive feedback trading: automatic sales triggered when prices fall reinforce the decline and drain liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A high concentration of trend-following and breakout strategies contributes to a stable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Trend and breakout trading are causes of positive feedback trading (buy as prices rise, sell as they fall), which destabilises prices and liquidity.
cards.originalText: A high concentration of trend-following and breakout strategies among participants.
cards.correction: A high concentration of trend-following and breakout strategies contributes to an unstable market with respect to liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A high concentration of trend-following and breakout strategies contributes to an unstable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Trend and breakout trading are causes of positive feedback trading (buy as prices rise, sell as they fall), which destabilises prices and liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Heavy use of programmes that synthetically create put options on portfolios contributes to a stable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Synthetically replicating portfolio puts requires selling after a price decline and buying after a rise; this portfolio insurance mechanism contributed to the October 1987 crash.
cards.originalText: Heavy use of programmes that synthetically create put options on participants' portfolios.
cards.correction: Heavy use of programmes that synthetically create put options on portfolios contributes to an unstable market with respect to liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Heavy use of programmes that synthetically create put options on portfolios contributes to an unstable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Synthetically replicating portfolio puts requires selling after a price decline and buying after a rise; this portfolio insurance mechanism contributed to the October 1987 crash.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A substantial presence of negative feedback traders, who buy when prices fall and sell when prices rise, contributes to a stable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Negative feedback traders create demand when prices are too low and supply when they are too high, keeping the market balanced and liquid.
cards.originalText: A substantial presence of negative feedback traders, who buy when prices fall and sell when prices rise.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Stop-loss rules that trigger automatic sales once a price falls below a set level are a cause of positive feedback trading.
cards.explanation: Stop-loss rules are a source of positive feedback trading that is always present in the market: falling prices trigger further sales.
cards.originalText: Stop-loss rules that trigger automatic sales once a price falls below a set level.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Margin calls on highly leveraged positions following a large adverse move in market variables are a cause of positive feedback trading.
cards.explanation: Margin calls force leveraged traders to close out positions, reinforcing the original move; exchanges raising margin requirements can worsen it further.
cards.originalText: Margin calls on highly leveraged positions following a large adverse move in market variables.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Dynamically hedging a long position in a call option is a cause of positive feedback trading.
cards.explanation: Delta hedging a long call requires selling after a rise and buying after a decline, which is negative feedback trading. It is dynamic hedging of a short position in calls or puts that causes positive feedback trading.
cards.originalText: Dynamically hedging a long position in a call option.
cards.correction: Dynamically hedging a long position in a call option is a cause of negative feedback trading.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Dynamically hedging a long position in a call option is a cause of negative feedback trading.
cards.explanation: Delta hedging a long call requires selling after a rise and buying after a decline, which is negative feedback trading. It is dynamic hedging of a short position in calls or puts that causes positive feedback trading.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Predatory trading ahead of a large liquidation that other participants have anticipated is a cause of positive feedback trading.
cards.explanation: Predatory traders sell ahead of an anticipated large liquidation, pushing prices further; this is also why large positions are usually unwound slowly.
cards.originalText: Predatory trading ahead of a large liquidation that other participants have anticipated.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: In a deleveraging cycle, forced asset sales depress prices, which raises investors' measured leverage and forces further sales.
cards.explanation: Falling prices erode equity faster than debt, so measured leverage rises and investors must sell more, making the deleveraging cycle self-reinforcing.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: In a deleveraging cycle, forced asset sales depress prices, which lowers investors' measured leverage, so the cycle is self-correcting.
cards.explanation: Forced sales depress prices, which raises measured leverage and forces further sales; the deleveraging cycle is self-reinforcing, not self-correcting.
cards.correction: In a deleveraging cycle, forced asset sales depress prices, which raises investors' measured leverage, so the cycle is self-reinforcing.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: In a deleveraging cycle, forced asset sales depress prices, which raises investors' measured leverage, so the cycle is self-reinforcing.
cards.explanation: Forced sales depress prices, which raises measured leverage and forces further sales; the deleveraging cycle is self-reinforcing, not self-correcting.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: In a leveraging cycle, rising asset prices raise investors' measured leverage, which obliges them to sell assets to restore their target ratios.
cards.explanation: Rising asset prices lower measured leverage, which permits further borrowing and further purchases in the leveraging cycle.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Hedge funds are largely insulated from the cycle, because prime brokers set leverage limits contractually in advance and cannot vary them during a stress.
cards.explanation: Prime brokers cut permitted hedge fund leverage sharply during the crisis, and hedge funds are particularly affected by the leveraging and deleveraging cycle.

cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Under an asset management strategy, the key control lever is price, meaning the interest rate and other terms offered on deposits and borrowings, used to achieve the desired volume, mix and cost of funds.
cards.explanation: Using price (rates and terms on deposits and borrowings) as the control lever over funding is the defining feature of liability management, not asset management.
cards.correction: Under a liability management strategy, the key control lever is price, meaning the interest rate and other terms offered on deposits and borrowings, used to achieve the desired volume, mix and cost of funds.

cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Under a liability management strategy, the amount and kinds of deposits the institution holds are treated as largely determined by its customers, so the only real decision area is the allocation of incoming funds.
cards.explanation: Treating deposits as customer-determined and confining management to the allocation of incoming funds is the asset management view; liability management seeks control over funding sources through price.
cards.correction: Under an asset management strategy, the amount and kinds of deposits the institution holds are treated as largely determined by its customers, so the only real decision area is the allocation of incoming funds.

cards.statement: Under a funds management strategy, control over assets must be coordinated with control over liabilities so that the two are internally consistent and do not pull against each other.
cards.explanation: Coordinating control over assets with control over liabilities so the two are internally consistent is one of the stated objectives of funds management, the approach that dominates today.

cards.statement: The asset-liability committee reports to the head of the risk function and its principal responsibility is approving individual credit exposures above a stated threshold.
cards.explanation: The ALCO reports the firm's financial condition to the board, and its remit covers interest rate and other risk exposures, funding plans and risk limits, not individual credit approvals.

cards.statement: Price risk arises when market interest rates fall, causing the market values of most bonds and fixed-rate loans to decline, so that sales in a falling rate period realise capital losses.
cards.explanation: Price risk arises when market interest rates rise, since that is when the values of bonds and fixed-rate loans fall and sales realise capital losses.
cards.correction: Price risk arises when market interest rates rise, causing the market values of most bonds and fixed-rate loans to decline, so that sales in a rising rate period realise capital losses.

cards.statement: Reinvestment risk arises when market interest rates rise, forcing the institution to place incoming funds in lower-yielding earning assets and reducing expected future income.
cards.explanation: Reinvestment risk arises when rates fall, forcing incoming funds into lower-yielding assets; if rates rise, incoming funds are placed at higher yields.
cards.correction: Reinvestment risk arises when market interest rates fall, forcing the institution to place incoming funds in lower-yielding earning assets and reducing expected future income.

cards.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Price risk arises when market interest rates rise and the institution must accept capital losses if it sells fixed-rate instruments; reinvestment risk arises when rates fall and incoming funds must be placed at lower yields.
cards.explanation: The two risks sit on opposite sides of the rate move: rising rates create price risk (capital losses on fixed-rate instruments) and falling rates create reinvestment risk (lower future income).

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Because a financial intermediary is usually on both the supply and the demand side of the loanable funds market at the same time, it can set the level of rates on its own loans and deposits and so neutralise both forms of risk.
cards.explanation: Financial institutions are price takers: each one, however large, is one participant among thousands in the loanable funds market, so it cannot set rate levels and neutralise both risks.

cards.statement: Market interest rates are set by the interactions of thousands of credit suppliers and demanders, and any particular rate is composed of a real risk-free rate plus several risk premiums, any of which can shift.
cards.explanation: Rates are set by the interaction of thousands of suppliers and demanders of loanable funds, and each rate combines a real risk-free rate with several risk premiums that can each shift, making consistently accurate forecasting virtually impossible.

cards.statement: A sufficiently large institution can influence the level of market interest rates through the scale of its own lending and deposit-taking, so forecasting is materially more tractable for large banks.
cards.explanation: Each institution, however large, is only one supplier and demander in an international market with many thousands of participants, so it cannot influence market rate levels.

cards.explanation: Under the Fisher effect the nominal rate equals the real rate plus expected inflation, which is why nominal rates move when inflation expectations move.

cards.statement: Nominal interest rates cannot fall below zero, which places a firm lower bound on the forecasting problem.
cards.explanation: Nominal rates can and have gone negative, for example in the 1930s, the 2003 repo market and the 2008 Treasury bill market.

cards.correction: Most lending institutions run a positive maturity gap, because their security holdings and loans mature later than the deposits and borrowings that fund them.

cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Most lending institutions run a positive maturity gap, so an upward-sloping yield curve tends to support a positive net interest margin, while a flat or negatively sloped curve compresses it.
cards.explanation: With assets longer than liabilities, an upward-sloping curve lets revenue from longer-term assets outstrip the cost of shorter-term liabilities; a flat or inverted curve squeezes the margin.

cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A negatively sloped yield curve is generally associated with rising interest rates and with expansion in the economy.
cards.explanation: An upward-sloping yield curve is associated with rising rates and expansion; a negatively sloped curve suggests falling rates and a possible recession.
cards.correction: An upward-sloping yield curve is generally associated with rising interest rates and with expansion in the economy.

cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A zero interest-sensitive gap fully immunises the net interest margin, because equal repricing volumes on the two sides guarantee that interest revenue and interest cost move together.
cards.explanation: A zero gap reduces but does not eliminate interest rate risk, because rates on assets and liabilities are not perfectly correlated; loan rates tend to lag money market rates even when repricing volumes match.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Interest rates paid on liabilities, which are mostly short term, tend to move faster than interest rates earned on assets, many of which are long term, so the interest-sensitive gap technique's implicit assumption of parallel repricing is imperfect.
cards.explanation: This is a stated limitation of interest-sensitive gap management: the liability side tends to reprice first, so the two sides do not move in step.
cards.originalText: Interest rates paid on liabilities, which are mostly short term, tend to move faster than interest rates earned on assets, many of which are long term, so the technique's implicit assumption of parallel repricing is imperfect.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Interest-sensitive gap management overstates a bank's exposure to rate movements because it captures the effect of those movements on both net income and the market value of shareholders' equity.
cards.explanation: Interest-sensitive gap management captures the effect of rate changes on net income only and ignores the market value of equity, so it understates the full exposure.
cards.originalText: The technique overstates a bank's exposure to rate movements because it captures the effect of those movements on both net income and the market value of shareholders' equity.
cards.correction: Interest-sensitive gap management understates a bank's exposure to rate movements because it captures the effect of those movements on net income but not the market value of shareholders' equity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk

cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Interest-sensitive gap management understates a bank's exposure to rate movements because it captures the effect of those movements on net income but not the market value of shareholders' equity.
cards.explanation: Interest-sensitive gap management captures the effect of rate changes on net income only and ignores the market value of equity, so it understates the full exposure.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: The repricing dates of checkable deposits and passbook savings accounts are fixed by contract, so the arbitrary choice of planning period is the only material source of imprecision in interest-sensitive gap management.
cards.explanation: Rates on checkable deposits and passbook savings can be adjusted at any time, so their repricing point is hard to pin down; the arbitrary planning period is only one of several limitations.
cards.originalText: The repricing dates of checkable deposits and passbook savings accounts are fixed by contract, so the arbitrary choice of planning period is the technique's only material source of imprecision.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A limitation of duration gap management is that finding assets and liabilities of the same duration that also fit the institution's portfolio is often a frustrating task.
cards.explanation: Matching durations while keeping a sensible portfolio is hard, and would be far easier if maturity equalled duration, which it generally does not.
cards.originalText: Finding assets and liabilities of the same duration that also fit the institution's portfolio is often a frustrating task.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A limitation of duration gap management is that duration itself shifts as market rates move and as instruments approach maturity, so a matched position requires continual and costly rebalancing.
cards.explanation: Immunisation is a dynamic problem: durations drift as instruments near maturity and as rates move, forcing costly portfolio restructuring.
cards.originalText: Duration itself shifts as market rates move and as instruments approach maturity, so a matched position requires continual and costly rebalancing.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Duration gap management analyses the effect of rate changes on the institution's net income while neglecting their effect on the market value of shareholders' equity.
cards.explanation: Ignoring the market value of equity is a limitation of interest-sensitive gap management; duration gap management was developed precisely to protect net worth.
cards.originalText: The technique analyses the effect of rate changes on the institution's net income while neglecting their effect on the market value of shareholders' equity.
cards.correction: Interest-sensitive gap management analyses the effect of rate changes on the institution's net income while neglecting their effect on the market value of shareholders' equity.

cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A limitation of duration gap management is that the model assumes a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, so its accuracy declines for large rate changes unless convexity is taken into account.
cards.explanation: Duration is a first-order (linear) approximation, so large rate moves require a convexity adjustment for accurate estimates.
cards.originalText: The model assumes a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, so its accuracy declines for large rate changes unless convexity is taken into account.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Because the duration gap model assumes a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, its accuracy declines as the size of the rate change grows, and for a positively convex position the model understates the gain from a rate fall and overstates the loss from a rate rise.
cards.explanation: Positive convexity puts the true price curve above the duration tangent on both sides, so the linear estimate is too low in each direction: it understates the gain and overstates the loss.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Because the duration gap model assumes a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, its accuracy declines as the size of the rate change grows, and for a positively convex position the model overstates the gain from a rate fall and understates the loss from a rate rise.
cards.explanation: For a positively convex position the linear duration estimate understates the gain from a rate fall and overstates the loss from a rate rise; the reverse pattern would indicate negative convexity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: The duration gap model's accuracy is unaffected by the size of the rate change but deteriorates when the yield curve shifts in parallel, since duration is defined only for non-parallel movements in rates.
cards.explanation: Accuracy declines as the size of the rate change grows, and duration assumes parallel shifts, so it is non-parallel movements that degrade it.
cards.originalText: The model's accuracy is unaffected by the size of the rate change but deteriorates when the yield curve shifts in parallel, since duration is defined only for non-parallel movements in rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Duration remains constant as instruments approach maturity, so a matched position established today requires no rebalancing for as long as the level of interest rates is unchanged.
cards.explanation: Duration changes as instruments approach maturity as well as when rates move, so immunisation is a dynamic problem requiring continual rebalancing.

cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A bank whose total assets exceed its total liabilities must by construction have a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap.
cards.explanation: Solvency concerns the relative amounts of assets and liabilities, while the duration gap concerns their timing; a solvent institution can have a positive, negative or zero leverage-adjusted duration gap.
cards.correction: A bank whose total assets exceed its total liabilities can have a positive, negative or zero leverage-adjusted duration gap.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
