cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Holding earning assets and cost of funds constant, a bank holding short-term floating-rate bonds with frequent coupon resets sees its NII and NIM increase in a rising interest rate environment.
cards.explanation: Coupons on quickly resetting floating-rate bonds rise with rates while interest expense is held constant, so net interest income rises, and with earning assets constant, the net interest margin rises too.
cards.originalText: NII and NIM will increase.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Holding earning assets and cost of funds constant, a bank holding short-term floating-rate bonds with frequent coupon resets sees its NII and NIM decline in a rising interest rate environment.
cards.explanation: Frequently resetting floating-rate bonds are rate-sensitive assets whose coupons rise with market rates. With funding cost fixed, NII and NIM increase rather than decline.
cards.originalText: NII and NIM will decline.
cards.correction: Holding earning assets and cost of funds constant, a bank holding short-term floating-rate bonds with frequent coupon resets sees its NII and NIM increase in a rising interest rate environment.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A bank holding mostly 30-year fixed-rate mortgages and funded mainly by repurchase agreements and one-quarter negotiable CDs has a negative 91-day interest-sensitive gap.
cards.explanation: Long-term fixed-rate mortgages do not reprice within 91 days, while repos and one-quarter CDs do, so rate-sensitive liabilities exceed rate-sensitive assets and the gap is negative.
cards.originalText: negative.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A bank holding mostly 30-year fixed-rate mortgages and funded mainly by repurchase agreements and one-quarter negotiable CDs has a positive 91-day interest-sensitive gap.
cards.explanation: The mortgages are not rate sensitive over 91 days while the short-term funding is, so the 91-day gap is negative (liability sensitive).
cards.originalText: positive.
cards.correction: A bank holding mostly 30-year fixed-rate mortgages and funded mainly by repurchase agreements and one-quarter negotiable CDs has a negative 91-day interest-sensitive gap.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A bank's interest-sensitive gap over a repricing bucket equals its duration gap.
cards.explanation: The interest-sensitive gap is a repricing measure in dollars over a time bucket, whereas the duration gap is a market-value measure. The two are different by definition.
cards.originalText: equal to its duration gap.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Other things equal, the net interest margin of a bank with a positive interest-sensitive gap increases as interest rates increase.
cards.explanation: With more assets than liabilities repricing, interest income responds more strongly to rate changes than interest expense, so the margin moves in the same direction as rates.
cards.originalText: increase as interest rates increase.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Other things equal, the net interest margin of a bank with a positive interest-sensitive gap increases as interest rates decrease.
cards.explanation: That is the effect for a negative-gap (liability-sensitive) bank. A positive-gap bank sees its margin fall when rates fall.
cards.originalText: increase as interest rates decrease.
cards.correction: Other things equal, the net interest margin of a bank with a positive interest-sensitive gap decreases as interest rates decrease.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Other things equal, the net interest margin of a bank with a positive interest-sensitive gap decreases as interest rates increase.
cards.explanation: That is the outcome for a negative-gap (liability-sensitive) bank. A positive-gap, asset-sensitive bank gains when rates rise.
cards.originalText: decrease as interest rates increase.
cards.correction: Other things equal, the net interest margin of a bank with a positive interest-sensitive gap increases as interest rates increase.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: For a bank with negative interest-sensitive gaps expecting rates to rise, increasing overnight fed funds borrowing and relying less on long-term Federal Home Loan Bank funding is an effective way to hedge net interest margin.
cards.explanation: Hedging a negative gap against rising rates requires fewer rate-sensitive liabilities or more rate-sensitive assets. Shifting from long-term to overnight funding does the opposite and widens the exposure.
cards.originalText: Increasing the volume of overnight funding from the fed funds market and relying less on long‑term funding from the Federal Home Loan Bank.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: For a bank with negative interest-sensitive gaps expecting rates to rise, selling long-term Treasury bonds and buying short-term Treasury bonds helps hedge net interest margin.
cards.explanation: Short-term securities reprice sooner, which raises rate-sensitive assets and moves the gap toward zero or positive.
cards.originalText: Selling long‑term Treasury bonds and purchasing short‑term Treasury bonds.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: For a bank with negative interest-sensitive gaps expecting rates to rise, shifting from making fixed-rate mortgages to making variable-rate mortgages helps hedge net interest margin.
cards.explanation: Variable-rate mortgages reprice upward as rates rise, which makes assets more rate sensitive and closes the negative gap.
cards.originalText: Shifting from a focus on making fixed‑rate mortgages to a focus on making variable‑rate mortgages.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: For a bank with negative interest-sensitive gaps expecting rates to rise, shifting funding from overnight repurchase agreements to five-year retail certificates of deposit helps hedge net interest margin.
cards.explanation: Locking in five-year funding removes liabilities from the rate-sensitive buckets, which reduces the negative gap.
cards.originalText: Shifting funding from overnight repurchase agreements to five‑year retail certificates of deposit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A firm using duration-gap analysis is fully hedged when it has a zero-duration gap position.
cards.explanation: With a zero leverage-adjusted duration gap, the dollar changes in asset and liability values offset for a given rate change, so net worth is protected.
cards.originalText: When fully hedged, it will have a zero‑duration gap position.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A firm using duration-gap analysis is fully hedged when it has higher interest-rate sensitive liabilities relative to its interest-rate sensitive assets.
cards.explanation: A liability-sensitive interest-sensitive gap position is an income exposure to rising rates, not evidence of a zero duration gap. A full hedge requires a zero leverage-adjusted duration gap.
cards.originalText: When it has higher interest‑rate sensitive liabilities relative to its interest‑rate sensitive assets.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Assets and liabilities exhibit higher sensitivity to changes in interest rates when the coupon is lower, the duration is higher, or the overall level of interest rates is lower.
cards.explanation: Value sensitivity rises with duration and is greater for low-coupon instruments and at low rate levels.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A non-prepayable loan has a lower duration than a prepayable mortgage loan, making it less sensitive to overall interest rate changes.
cards.explanation: Prepayments shorten a mortgage's duration, so the non-prepayable loan has the higher duration and is the more rate sensitive of the two.
cards.originalText: A non‑prepayable loan has a lower duration compared to a prepayable mortgage loan, making it less sensitive to overall interest rate changes.
cards.correction: A non-prepayable loan has a higher duration than a prepayable mortgage loan, making it more sensitive to overall interest rate changes.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Paying a cash dividend of USD 50 million out of cash has no impact on a bank's overall asset duration.
cards.explanation: Cash has zero duration, so removing it shrinks the asset base and changes the dollar-weighted average duration of the remaining assets.
cards.originalText: Paying a cash dividend of USD 50 million using cash will have no impact on the overall asset duration of the bank.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A bank holding mostly 30-year fixed-rate mortgages and funded mainly by repurchase agreements and negotiable CDs, with assets about 10% greater than liabilities, has a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap.
cards.explanation: Asset duration is long and liability duration is short, and the liability duration is scaled down further by the leverage ratio, so the leverage-adjusted gap is clearly positive.
cards.originalText: positive.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A bank's leverage-adjusted duration gap equals its unadjusted duration gap.
cards.explanation: The leverage-adjusted gap equals the plain gap only if liabilities equal assets, that is when $L/A = 1$. With equity in the capital structure the two differ.
cards.originalText: equal to its duration gap.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
cards.statement: The normal-market cost of liquidation charges half of each position's current proportional spread on its mid-market value, while the stressed cost replaces that spread with its mean plus a confidence multiple of its standard deviation.
cards.explanation: In normal conditions the cost is the sum of half the proportional spread times the position value. In stressed conditions the spread is replaced by $\mu + \lambda\sigma$, where the multiple $\lambda$ sets the required confidence level.
cards.originalText: The normal-market cost charges half of each position’s current proportional spread on its mid-market value, while the stressed cost replaces that spread with its mean plus a confidence multiple of its standard deviation.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
cards.statement: The stressed cost of liquidation assumes spreads on all instruments are perfectly correlated, so it overstates liquidity risk and should be reduced to reflect diversification across positions.
cards.explanation: The perfect-correlation assumption may seem overly conservative, but it is not: spreads tend to widen together when liquidity is tight, so diversification does not necessarily reduce liquidity trading risk.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
cards.statement: Allowing more days to unwind a book lowers both the bid-offer spread cost and the exposure to adverse mid-market moves, so the longest feasible liquidation horizon should always be assumed.
cards.explanation: A longer horizon lowers the spread cost but raises the risk of adverse mid-market moves, which is why the liquidation schedule is optimised rather than always stretched.
cards.originalText: Allowing more days to unwind the book lowers both the bid-offer spread cost and the exposure to adverse mid-market moves, so the longest feasible liquidation horizon should always be assumed.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
cards.statement: If a book is liquidated in equal parts over $T$ days, its liquidity-adjusted VaR equals the one-day VaR scaled by the square root of $T$, because the whole position stays exposed for all $T$ days.
cards.explanation: The position shrinks each day, so only a declining fraction is exposed. The scaling factor is $\sqrt{(1+T)(1+2T)/(6T)}$, so $\sqrt{T}$ overstates the liquidity-adjusted VaR.
cards.originalText: If the book is liquidated in equal parts over $T$ days, its liquidity-adjusted VaR equals the one-day VaR scaled by the square root of $T$ , because the whole position stays exposed for all $T$ days.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Interest on municipal bonds issued for public projects is exempt from federal income tax, but capital gains on municipals are taxable, apart from the accretion to par on bonds bought at a discount.
cards.explanation: Interest on municipals issued for public projects is exempt, but capital gains are taxable. The one exception is the gain from purchase price to par on a discount bond, which counts as part of tax-exempt interest.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Municipal bonds are fully tax-exempt on interest and on capital gains alike.
cards.explanation: Only the interest on qualifying municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax. Capital gains on municipals are taxable, with a limited exception for accretion on discount bonds.
cards.originalText: Municipal bonds are fully tax-exempt, on interest and on capital gains alike, which is why high-bracket banks prefer them to Treasury bonds.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Revenue bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the issuing government and may be repaid from any source of revenue, including new taxes.
cards.explanation: Full faith and credit backing and repayment from any revenue describe general obligation bonds. Revenue bonds are payable only from stipulated sources.
cards.correction: General obligation bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the issuing government and may be repaid from any source of revenue, including new taxes.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Corporate notes and bonds appeal more to banks than to insurance companies and pension funds.
cards.explanation: Corporate notes and bonds are more attractive to insurers and pension funds than to banks, because of their higher credit risk and more limited resale market.
cards.originalText: Corporate notes and bonds appeal more to banks than to insurance companies and pension funds, because their resale market is deeper than that of government securities.
cards.correction: Corporate notes and bonds appeal more to insurance companies and pension funds than to banks.

changes.from: banks than to insurance companies and pension funds
changes.to: insurance companies and pension funds than to banks

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Principal-only strips are more price-sensitive to interest-rate changes than the underlying bonds, while interest-only strips are less price-sensitive.
cards.explanation: A principal-only strip is a single deep-discount payment far in the future, so it is more price sensitive than a regular bond. An interest-only strip tends to be less price sensitive.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Mortgage-backed bonds remove the pledged mortgages from the issuer's balance sheet, in the same way as pass-through securities.
cards.explanation: Pass-throughs and CMOs take the mortgages off the balance sheet, but mortgage-backed bonds keep the segregated, pledged mortgages on it.
cards.originalText: Mortgage-backed bonds remove the pledged mortgages from the issuer’s balance sheet, in the same way as pass-through securities.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Both principal-only and interest-only strips pay periodic coupons, so they carry the same reinvestment risk as the underlying Treasury bond.
cards.explanation: Treasury strips are zero-coupon securities with no interim payments, so they carry zero reinvestment risk.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Structured notes are plain fixed-rate agency notes.
cards.explanation: Structured notes carry reset, cap, floor or step-up coupons. Their complexity has resulted in substantial losses for some investing institutions.
cards.originalText: Structured notes are plain fixed-rate agency notes, which is why investing institutions suffered few losses on them when rates moved in the 1990s.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: For a bank in the 35% federal tax bracket, a tax-exempt municipal note yielding 4.55% is equivalent to a fully taxable security yielding 2.96%.
cards.explanation: The tax-equivalent yield is $4.55\%/(1-0.35) = 7.00\%$, so a taxable security must yield 7.00% before tax to match the note. Multiplying by $(1-t)$ instead of dividing gives the wrong answer.
cards.originalText: A tax-exempt municipal note yielding 4.55% is worth the same to the bank as a fully taxable security yielding 2.96%, so taxable Treasuries above that yield are preferable.
cards.correction: For a bank in the 35% federal tax bracket, a tax-exempt municipal note yielding 4.55% is equivalent to a fully taxable security yielding 7.00%.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Eurocurrency deposits are insured in the same way as domestic CDs.
cards.explanation: Deposit insurance belongs to domestic CDs. Eurocurrency deposits are not insured and, because of their higher perceived credit risk, often carry slightly higher yields than domestic time deposits.
cards.originalText: Eurocurrency deposits are insured in the same way as domestic CDs, so they usually yield slightly less than time deposits of comparable-size US banks.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Adding a large volume of liquid, readily marketable securities raises the average yield on earning assets.
cards.explanation: Buying a large volume of liquid, readily marketable securities tends to lower the average yield and profitability, so management faces a trade-off between liquidity and profitability.
cards.originalText: Adding a large volume of liquid, readily marketable securities raises the average yield on earning assets, because it lowers the bank’s exposure to liquidity risk.
cards.correction: Adding a large volume of liquid, readily marketable securities lowers the average yield on earning assets.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Buying investment-grade municipals issued outside a bank's home region helps offset business risk in its local loan book, and banks are generally limited to securities rated Baa/BBB or better.
cards.explanation: Business risk is the risk that the local economy turns down, which shows up quickly in the loan book, so out-of-market purchases help offset it. Regulation generally lets banks buy only investment-grade securities.
cards.originalText: Buying investment-grade municipals issued outside the bank’s home region helps offset business risk in the local loan book, and banks are generally limited to Baa/BBB or better.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Prepayments on mortgage-backed securities accelerate when market interest rates rise, because borrowers refinance into new loans.
cards.explanation: Refinancing accelerates when market interest rates fall, not when they rise.
cards.correction: Prepayments on mortgage-backed securities accelerate when market interest rates fall, because borrowers refinance into new loans.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Public deposits above the insured amount must be backed by pledged Treasury and agency securities valued at par, while eligible municipals are usually valued at a discount from par.
cards.explanation: The uninsured part of public deposits must be collateralised by Treasury and federal agency securities at par. Eligible municipal bonds can also be pledged, but they are valued at a discount, often 80 to 90 percent of face value.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: TIPS protect against inflation by adjusting only the coupon to the CPI, while the principal stays fixed at par.
cards.explanation: TIPS adjust the principal (face) value to the CPI, and the coupon payments, being a fixed rate on the adjusted principal, move with it.
cards.correction: TIPS protect against inflation by adjusting the principal to the CPI, with the coupon payments moving with it.

changes.from: adjusting only the coupon to the CPI, while the principal stays fixed at par
changes.to: adjusting the principal to the CPI, with the coupon payments moving with it

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
cards.statement: Business risk is best offset by concentrating security purchases on issuers in the bank's own market area.
cards.explanation: Business risk is offset by buying securities from issuers outside the bank's loan market, which is why examiners encourage out-of-market purchases.
cards.originalText: Business risk is best offset by concentrating security purchases on issuers in the bank’s own market area, whose finances its lending oﬀicers know well.
cards.correction: Business risk is best offset by concentrating security purchases on issuers outside the bank's own market area.

changes.from: in the bank's own market area
changes.to: outside the bank's own market area

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: When market interest rates rise sharply, customers speed up drawings on credit lines that carry lower interest rates, while assets the bank may need to sell fall in value and borrowed liquidity costs more.
cards.explanation: Rising rates increase demands for liquidity through faster credit-line drawings and raise the cost of meeting them, because asset values fall and borrowing becomes more expensive.
cards.originalText: Customers speed up drawings on credit lines that carry lower interest rates, while assets the bank may need to sell fall in value and borrowed liquidity costs more.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: When market interest rates rise, deposit withdrawals slow because higher market rates make a bank's existing deposits more attractive to customers.
cards.explanation: Higher market rates draw deposits away as some customers withdraw funds in search of higher returns elsewhere, so withdrawals tend to speed up.
cards.originalText: Deposit withdrawals slow, because higher market rates make the bank’s existing deposits more attractive to customers.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: When market interest rates rise, loan customers bring forward new loan requests, while the market value of the bank's securities available for sale rises.
cards.explanation: Customers tend to postpone new loan requests when rates rise, and the market value of securities falls when rates rise.
cards.originalText: Loan customers bring forward new loan requests, while the market value of the bank’s securities available for sale rises.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Rising interest rates leave a bank's liquidity needs unchanged, because interest rate movements affect only profitability, not cash flows.
cards.explanation: Rate changes alter deposit and loan demand, and so a bank's cash flows and liquidity needs, not only its profit.
cards.originalText: Liquidity needs are unchanged, because interest rate movements affect only the bank’s profitability, not its cash flows.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: The more resources a bank ties up in readiness to meet liquidity demands, the lower its expected profitability, other factors held constant.
cards.explanation: There is a trade-off between liquidity and profitability: liquid holdings earn little, so resources tied up for liquidity reduce expected profit.
cards.originalText: The more resources the bank ties up in readiness to meet liquidity demands, the lower its expected profitability, other factors held constant.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: A bank should aim to keep supplies of liquidity exactly equal to demands at every moment, so that it is never in surplus or deficit.
cards.explanation: Supplies and demands for liquidity are rarely equal at any particular moment. The goal of liquidity management is to manage the gap, not to abolish it.
cards.originalText: The bank should aim to keep supplies of liquidity exactly equal to demands at every moment, so that it is never in surplus or deficit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Most liquidity problems originate inside the bank.
cards.explanation: Most liquidity problems arise from outside the financial firm, as a result of the activities of its customers.
cards.originalText: Because most liquidity problems originate inside the bank, tight internal cost control is the main defence against them.
cards.correction: Most liquidity problems originate outside the bank.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: A liquidity surplus carries no cost, so excess funds can wait until the next scheduled investment date.
cards.explanation: Excess liquidity has an opportunity cost, so surplus funds should be invested immediately.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Borrowed liquidity (liability management) is the less risky liquidity strategy and the one smaller institutions mainly use.
cards.explanation: Borrowing liquidity is the most risky approach, though it carries the highest expected return, and it is used most by the largest banks. Asset conversion is the less risky approach used mainly by smaller institutions.
cards.originalText: Cover the CAD 90 million deficit by borrowing, since liability management is the less risky strategy and the one smaller institutions mainly use.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Selling Treasury bills to meet a liquidity need leaves the size and composition of the bank's asset portfolio unchanged.
cards.explanation: Leaving the asset portfolio unchanged is an advantage of borrowed liquidity. Selling assets shrinks the size of the firm and changes its asset mix.
cards.originalText: Cover the CAD 90 million deficit by selling Treasury bills, since this leaves the size and composition of the bank’s asset portfolio unchanged.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Holding marketable securities in excess of a projected liquidity deficit guarantees that a bank is liquid whatever demands it faces.
cards.explanation: A firm holding more liquid assets will not necessarily be a liquid institution, because its position also depends on the demands made against it. Liquidity means access to funds at reasonable cost at precisely the time they are needed.
cards.originalText: Treat the CAD 90 million deficit as no concern, since securities holdings above the deficit guarantee the bank is liquid whatever demands it faces.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: A drawback of asset conversion as a liquidity strategy is that the cost of the funds raised is always uncertain, which adds uncertainty to earnings.
cards.explanation: Uncertain cost of funds is a drawback of borrowed liquidity, not of asset conversion. The cost of selling an asset is largely known when it is sold.
cards.originalText: The cost of the funds raised is always uncertain, which adds uncertainty to earnings.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: A cost of asset conversion as a liquidity strategy is the loss of the future earnings that the sold assets would have generated.
cards.explanation: This opportunity cost is why assets with the least profit potential should be sold first.
cards.originalText: The future earnings the sold assets would have generated are lost.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Asset conversion as a liquidity strategy involves commissions paid to security brokers, and the assets may have to be sold into a falling market.
cards.explanation: Transactions costs and the risk of selling into declining prices are both recognised drawbacks of asset conversion.
cards.originalText: Commissions are paid to security brokers, and the assets may have to be sold into a falling market.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Selling low-risk securities to raise liquidity weakens the appearance of a bank's balance sheet.
cards.explanation: The securities sold are often low-risk ones that give the impression that the firm is strong, so selling them makes the balance sheet look weaker.
cards.originalText: Selling low-risk securities weakens the appearance of the balance sheet.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: A money-center bank may borrow close to 100% of its liquidity needs, accepting the most risky approach in exchange for the highest expected return.
cards.explanation: Liability management techniques are used most extensively by the largest banks. Borrowing liquidity is the most risky approach but also carries the highest expected return.
cards.originalText: The money-center bank may borrow close to 100% of its liquidity needs, accepting the most risky approach in exchange for the highest expected return.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Smaller banks are more likely than the largest banks to rely on borrowed liquidity, because they find it the less risky approach.
cards.explanation: Smaller institutions rely on asset conversion, which they find less risky. Borrowed liquidity is the most risky approach and is used most by the largest banks.
cards.originalText: The community bank is more likely to rely on borrowed liquidity, because smaller banks find it the less risky approach.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Borrowed liquidity is the safest liquidity approach, because the bank borrows only when funds are actually needed.
cards.explanation: Borrowing only when needed is an advantage, but borrowed liquidity is nevertheless the most risky approach, mainly because its cost is uncertain and funds may not be available.
cards.originalText: Borrowed liquidity is the safest approach, because the bank borrows only when funds are actually needed.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Asset conversion carries the highest expected return among liquidity strategies, because the bank keeps control of its offer rate.
cards.explanation: Liquid assets carry the lowest returns, and control of the offer rate is a feature of liability management. Borrowed liquidity carries the highest expected return.
cards.originalText: Asset conversion carries the highest expected return, because the bank keeps control of its offer rate.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Under a balanced liquidity management strategy, expected demands for liquidity are met from marketable securities, other anticipated needs from prearranged lines of credit, and unexpected needs from near-term borrowings.
cards.explanation: A balanced strategy stores expected demands in marketable securities, backstops other anticipated needs with advance credit-line arrangements, and meets unexpected cash needs from near-term borrowing.
cards.originalText: Expected demands from marketable securities, other anticipated needs from prearranged lines of credit, and unexpected needs from near-term borrowings.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Under a balanced liquidity management strategy, expected demands for liquidity are met from near-term borrowings and unexpected needs from a storehouse of marketable securities.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed. Expected demands are stored in marketable securities, and it is the unexpected needs that are met by near-term borrowing.
cards.originalText: Expected demands from near-term borrowings, and unexpected needs from a storehouse of marketable securities.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: The liquidity manager should track the activities of all departments that use or supply funds, such as new credit lines granted by the loan department.
cards.explanation: Whenever the loan department grants a new credit line, the liquidity manager must prepare for possible drawings against it.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: Liquidity needs should be reviewed at the end of each quarter, since more frequent analysis adds cost without benefit.
cards.explanation: Liquidity needs must be analysed on a continuing basis, because excess liquidity not reinvested promptly loses income.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.loText: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.
cards.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
cards.statement: The plans of the largest funds-supplying customers are confidential to relationship managers and need not be known in advance by the liquidity manager.
cards.explanation: The liquidity manager should know in advance when the biggest credit and funds-supplying customers plan to withdraw or add funds.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
cards.statement: Security lending is the only contract on assets that decreases LGC, because possession passes, no cash is received, and the asset cannot raise liquidity until it is returned.
cards.explanation: The lent asset cannot be sold or pledged until it comes back and no principal is received, so security lending reduces liquidity generation capacity. Every other contract on assets either generates liquidity or leaves the asset available.
cards.originalText: Security lending is the only contract on assets that decreases LGC: possession passes, no cash is received, and the asset cannot raise liquidity until it is returned.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
cards.statement: In a repo, the coupons paid during the contract are removed from the TSECF, because possession passes to the counterparty.
cards.explanation: In a repo the bank keeps ownership, so the coupons remain its own and the TSECF is unaffected. Only possession passes.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
cards.statement: In a sell/buyback, the TSAA is unchanged, because the bank has committed to buy the asset back.
cards.explanation: In a sell/buyback possession and ownership both pass, so the TSAA falls by the notional until the buyback.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
cards.statement: Eurodollar borrowings trade in multiples of USD 1 million and are usually available only to money-centre banks with top ratings, while Fed funds and the discount window can make small loans.
cards.explanation: Size of the borrowing institution is a factor in choosing a nondeposit source. Eurodollar borrowings are standard in USD 1 million units for the highest-rated money-center firms, whereas Fed funds and the discount window can make relatively small loans.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
cards.statement: Overnight Fed funds offer the most predictable cost, because the shorter the term of a money market borrowing, the less volatile its interest rate tends to be.
cards.explanation: The shorter the term of the loan, the more volatile the prevailing market interest rate tends to be. Overnight Fed funds have the most volatile rate of all, which is their key disadvantage.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
cards.statement: Seasonal credit carries the highest of the three discount window rates.
cards.explanation: Secondary credit carries the highest of the three discount window rates, not seasonal credit.
cards.originalText: Seasonal credit carries the highest of the three discount window rates, so a sound bank needing funds today should request primary credit instead.
cards.correction: Secondary credit carries the highest of the three discount window rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
cards.statement: Negotiable CDs are legally deposits, so unlike Eurodollar borrowings and commercial paper they carry no credit availability risk for the issuing bank.
cards.explanation: The negotiable CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets are all especially sensitive to credit availability risk. Being legally a deposit does not protect an issuer from credit rationing.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: The effective Fed funds rate is usually among the cheapest short-term borrowing rates, although the rate on the shortest-term Treasury bills is often slightly lower.
cards.explanation: The prevailing effective Fed funds rate is usually among the cheapest sources of short-term borrowed funds, with domestic CDs, Eurocurrency deposits and commercial paper normally slightly higher.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: The primary credit rate at the discount window is normally among the cheapest short-term borrowing rates, because the Federal Reserve prices it below its target for the Fed funds rate.
cards.explanation: Since 2003 the primary credit rate has been set above the Fed funds target, which puts it among the highest short-term borrowing rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: Commercial paper is normally issued at rates below the Fed funds and CD rates.
cards.explanation: Commercial paper normally issues slightly above the Fed funds and CD rates. Being sold at a discount is how it is quoted, not why it is cheap.
cards.originalText: Commercial paper is normally issued at rates below the Fed funds and CD rates, because it is sold at a discount from face value.
cards.correction: Commercial paper is normally issued at rates slightly above the Fed funds and CD rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: Nondeposit funds generally cost less than checkable deposits but more than time and savings deposits, and their cost is more stable from year to year.
cards.explanation: Nondeposit funds generally cost more than checkable deposits and less than thrift deposits, and their costs are more volatile from year to year.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: The negotiable CD and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive to credit availability risk, so a bank should be prepared to switch to other sources and pay more if lenders ration credit.
cards.explanation: There is no guarantee that lenders will accommodate every borrower. When credit is tight it is rationed, and funds managers must be ready to switch sources and, if necessary, pay more.
cards.originalText: The negotiable CD and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive to credit availability risk, so the bank should be prepared to switch to other sources and pay more if lenders ration credit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: The effective Fed funds rate is set by the central bank and does not fluctuate around its target.
cards.explanation: The effective Fed funds rate fluctuates around the target, widely on settlement days. Only the central bank's own discount rate is administered.
cards.originalText: Fed funds carry the least interest rate risk of the three, because overnight rates are set by the central bank and do not fluctuate around its target.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: Credit availability risk is negligible for a profitable bank, because money market lenders accommodate every borrower willing to pay the market rate.
cards.explanation: Lenders may deny credit to a borrower that looks risky, or price it so high that earnings suffer, even when the borrower is willing to pay the market rate.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: The longer the term of a money market borrowing, the more volatile its interest rate tends to be.
cards.explanation: The shorter the term of the borrowing, the more volatile the prevailing market interest rate tends to be, so overnight borrowing is the most volatile.
cards.originalText: Interest rate risk rises with the term of the borrowing, so the three-month CD has the most volatile rate of the three sources.
cards.correction: The shorter the term of a money market borrowing, the more volatile its interest rate tends to be.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: Regulation can limit the amount, frequency and use of borrowed funds: US CDs must have a maturity of at least seven days, the Fed may limit window borrowing by risky banks, and reserve requirements were once imposed on Fed funds, RPs and commercial paper.
cards.explanation: Federal and state regulations may restrict how much, how often and for what purpose a bank borrows, which is one factor in choosing a nondeposit source.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: Under the customer relationship doctrine, the bank first decides how much it can raise in deposits and then approves only the loans those deposits can fund.
cards.explanation: Under the customer relationship doctrine, lending decisions come before funding decisions. If deposits fall short, the bank borrows the lowest-cost funds available.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: Liability management makes a bank's cost of funds less sensitive to market interest rates, because the bank rather than the depositor chooses the amount and the term.
cards.explanation: Liability management is an interest-sensitive approach: money market lenders are highly rate elastic and leave quickly if the bank will not pay the going rate. The borrower does gain flexibility over amount and term.
cards.originalText: Liability management makes the bank’s cost of funds less sensitive to market interest rates, because the bank rather than the depositor chooses the amount and the term.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
cards.statement: Because negotiable CDs are legally deposits, they carry the same 10% reserve requirement as checking accounts at the largest banks.
cards.explanation: The legal reserve requirement on negotiable CDs is currently zero, against 10% on checking accounts at the largest institutions.
cards.originalText: Because negotiable CDs are legally deposits, they carry the same 10% reserve requirement as checking accounts at the largest banks, which is why CDs cost more than Fed funds.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
cards.reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.statement: Under the matched-maturity marginal cost approach, a five-year bullet loan is charged the five-year term liquidity premium and a five-year term deposit is credited the same premium.
cards.explanation: A five-year bullet needs funding for its whole life and is charged the five-year premium, while a five-year term deposit provides five years of funding and is credited the same premium.
cards.originalText: Adopt matched-maturity marginal cost, so a five-year bullet loan is charged the 40 bp five-year term liquidity premium and a five-year term deposit is credited the same premium.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
cards.reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.statement: A single pooled average rate overcharges long-term loans and so discourages business units from excessive maturity transformation.
cards.explanation: A single average rate undercharges long-term assets and so promotes maturity transformation, because it ignores the heightened liquidity risk of longer-term assets.
cards.originalText: Retain the pooled average cost, because the flat 8 bp rate overcharges long-term loans and so discourages business units from excessive maturity transformation.
cards.correction: A single pooled average rate undercharges long-term loans and so promotes excessive maturity transformation by business units.

changes.from: overcharges long-term loans and so discourages business units from
changes.to: undercharges long-term loans and so promotes

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
cards.reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.statement: The cost of carrying the liquidity cushion should be kept in central treasury as an opportunity cost, rather than charged to the business units that use contingent liquidity.
cards.explanation: The cost of carry is a cost of doing business that should not be borne by central treasury. It should be recouped from the business activities that create the need, according to their predicted use of contingent liquidity.
cards.originalText: Keep the cost of carrying the liquidity cushion in central treasury as an opportunity cost, rather than charging it to the business units that use contingent liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
cards.reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
cards.statement: The funding charge on assets held in the liquidity cushion should be based on overnight rates, because those assets can be sold immediately in any market disruption.
cards.explanation: Charges on cushion assets should be derived from longer-term rates, not short-term overnight rates, to account for the possibility of longer than expected market disruptions.
cards.originalText: Price the funding of assets held in the liquidity cushion at overnight rates, because those assets can be sold immediately in any market disruption.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: A leading indicator provides information on significant potential stress before an actual event occurs.
cards.explanation: Leading indicators give a warning signal before the event, which is why leading early warning indicators are much more effective than lagging ones.
cards.originalText: Leading indicator

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: A lagging indicator provides information on significant potential stress before an actual event occurs.
cards.explanation: Lagging indicators signal only after the event has occurred, which is the opposite of an early warning.
cards.originalText: Lagging indicator
cards.correction: A leading indicator provides information on significant potential stress before an actual event occurs.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: A sharp early warning indicator is a highly granular indicator involving a subset of data.
cards.explanation: Sharpness means granularity: focusing on a specific subset of data so that the signal is not drowned out by noise. A fall in deposits of one client group is sharper than a fall in total deposits.
cards.originalText: A highly granular indicator, involving a subset of data

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: A sharp early warning indicator is one that highlights past performance.
cards.explanation: Indicators of past performance are lagging. A sharp indicator is a granular one that focuses on a subset of data.
cards.originalText: An indicator that highlights past performance

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: A sharp early warning indicator is one that depends on another performance measure.
cards.explanation: Dependence on another measure has nothing to do with sharpness, which means granularity.
cards.originalText: An indicator that depends on another performance measure

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: Good early warning indicator measures are forward-looking and sharp, meaning granular and specific.
cards.explanation: Good measures are leading and granular, covering internal and external factors, normal and stressed states, and several horizons.
cards.originalText: Forward‑looking and sharp (i.e., granular and specific)

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: Good early warning indicator measures include only internal measures and not external ones.
cards.explanation: Measures should include both internal (balance sheet) and external (macroeconomic) factors.
cards.originalText: Only internal but not external measures

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: Good early warning indicator measures are disassociated from the escalation process.
cards.explanation: Measures must be linked to escalation. Otherwise early warning indicators have no effect on liquidity risk management.
cards.originalText: Measures are disassociated (de‑linked) from the escalation process
cards.correction: Good early warning indicator measures are linked to the escalation process.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: Good early warning indicator measures are tracked in business-as-usual environments but should not be affected by stressed environments.
cards.explanation: Stressed states must also be examined to test whether liquid resources are sufficient, so measures should cover both normal and stressed conditions.
cards.originalText: Measures are tracked during business‑as‑usual environments but should not be affected by stressed environments

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: To be effective, early warning indicators must be tied to a definitive escalation plan.
cards.explanation: An early warning indicator only produces action when a breach triggers a definitive escalation path to the relevant management personnel. Without escalation it is just information.
cards.originalText: To be effective, EWIs must be tied to a definitive escalation plan.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: The more granular an early warning indicator is, the more accurate it is.
cards.explanation: Granularity makes an indicator sharper, meaning it is harder to lose in noise, but it does not make the indicator more accurate. Sharpness and accuracy are different properties.
cards.originalText: The more granular the indicator, the more accurate it is.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: Early warning indicators should focus on external metrics rather than internal metrics because external metrics are generally more reliable.
cards.explanation: Sound early warning indicators combine internal and external measures. Internal measures are valuable because they can reveal stress before it is visible externally.
cards.originalText: EWIs should focus on external metrics over internal metrics because the former are generally more reliable.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: Lagging indicators are less prone to error than leading indicators, so they are potentially more useful to liquidity risk managers.
cards.explanation: Lagging indicators signal only after the event, so they are much less effective than leading indicators for liquidity risk management. A lower error rate does not offset their lateness.
cards.originalText: Lagging indicators are less prone to error than leading indicators; therefore, they are potentially more useful to liquidity risk managers.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
cards.statement: Early warning indicator metrics are most valuable when they are tracked during a business-as-usual environment.
cards.explanation: Early warning only has value if the signal arrives while there is still time to act. This means monitoring the indicators continuously in normal conditions, not waiting for stress or a loss event.
cards.originalText: During a business‑as‑usual environment

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: Widening spreads on a bank's issued debt and credit default swaps are an early warning indicator of potential liquidity risk.
cards.explanation: Widening spreads on the bank's own debt and CDS are listed as early warning indicators by the OCC and the Federal Reserve. They show deteriorating market confidence before funding is lost.
cards.originalText: The spreads on the bank’s issued debt and credit default swaps have widened.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: Substantial asset growth financed by an expansion in stable liabilities is an early warning sign of potential liquidity risk.
cards.explanation: Rapid asset growth is a BCBS warning sign only when it is funded by potentially volatile liabilities. Funding the growth with stable liabilities mitigates the liquidity risk.
cards.originalText: The bank’s assets have grown substantially, and the growth has been financed by an expansion in stable liabilities.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: A longer average maturity of a bank's liabilities and more diversified funding sources are early warning signs of potential liquidity risk.
cards.explanation: Longer liability maturities and more diversified funding are improvements in liquidity risk. The BCBS warning signs are shorter liability durations and more concentrated funding.
cards.originalText: The average maturity of the bank’s liabilities has lengthened and its funding sources have become more diversified.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: A narrowing of debt or credit default swap spreads is an early warning sign of liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: The warning signal is a widening of debt and CDS spreads, which reflects deteriorating market confidence. Narrowing spreads indicate lower perceived risk.
cards.originalText: Narrowing of debt or credit default swap spreads
cards.correction: A widening of debt or credit default swap spreads is an early warning sign of liquidity stress.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: Increases in currency mismatches are an early warning sign of liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: Growing currency mismatches are listed as an early warning indicator in the BCBS (2008) guidance.
cards.originalText: Increases in currency mismatches

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: A drop in credit lines is an early warning sign of liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: Reduced financing from lenders, such as falling credit lines, is an OCC (2012) early warning indicator of liquidity stress.
cards.originalText: Drop in credit lines

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: Increasing redemptions of certificates of deposit before maturity are an early warning sign of liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: Early redemption of CDs signals deposit flight, which is a warning sign of funding stress.
cards.originalText: Increasing redemptions of CDs before maturity

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: An increase in asset quality is an early warning indicator of liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: Early warning indicators flag deteriorating conditions. Improving asset quality is a positive development, whereas deteriorating asset quality would be a warning sign.
cards.originalText: An increase in asset quality
cards.correction: A deterioration in asset quality is an early warning indicator of liquidity stress.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: A spike in market volatility is an early warning indicator of liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: A volatility spike is an adverse market condition and is treated as an early warning indicator.
cards.originalText: A spike in the market volatility

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: Real or perceived negative publicity is an early warning indicator of liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: Negative publicity, whether real or perceived, can trigger funding runs and is listed as an early warning indicator in Federal Reserve SR 10-6.
cards.originalText: Real or perceived negative publicity

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: A rapid rise in leverage combined with heavy reliance on short-term repo funding is an early warning indicator of potential liquidity problems.
cards.explanation: Rapid balance-sheet growth funded by short-term repo creates rollover risk. It matches the BCBS early warning indicators of sharp asset growth and shortened liability duration.
cards.originalText: A rapid rise in the leverage ratio and heavy reliance on short‑term repo funding.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: A reduction in the collateral haircuts imposed on a bank's collateralized exposures is an early warning indicator of potential liquidity problems.
cards.explanation: Lower haircuts make it easier to fund against collateral. A rise in haircuts, not a reduction, is the warning sign.
cards.originalText: A reduction in the collateral haircuts imposed on the bank’s collateralized exposures.
cards.correction: An increase in the collateral haircuts imposed on a bank's collateralized exposures is an early warning indicator of potential liquidity problems.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: An upward revision in a bank's credit rating is an early warning indicator of potential liquidity problems.
cards.explanation: A rating upgrade is favourable. Rating downgrades are the early warning indicators.
cards.originalText: An upward revision in the credit rating.
cards.correction: A downward revision in a bank's credit rating is an early warning indicator of potential liquidity problems.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: Increased diversification of assets is an early warning indicator of potential liquidity problems.
cards.explanation: Diversification reduces concentration risk. More concentrated assets or liabilities, not more diversified ones, are the warning sign.
cards.originalText: Increased diversification of assets.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: A sudden increase in debt costs is a red-flag indicator in a liquidity early warning dashboard.
cards.explanation: Rising borrowing costs and spread increases are OCC (2012) early warning indicators of liquidity stress.
cards.originalText: Sudden increase in debt costs.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
cards.statement: Sudden asset growth accompanied by volatile liabilities is a red-flag indicator in a liquidity early warning dashboard.
cards.explanation: Very sharp asset growth funded by volatile liabilities is a BCBS (2008) early warning indicator.
