cards.explanation: Funding trades are mostly general collateral, but for a special issue the holder lends the security in the specials market and borrows cash at a rate below general collateral, which lowers financing cost.
cards.originalText: Lend the note in the specials market at 0.09%, because the demand to borrow the note lets its holder borrow cash below the GC rate.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: The on-the-run Treasury usually trades special because most Treasury shorts are held briefly and prefer the most liquid issue, so they can cover quickly and cheaply, while holders of that issue require compensation for giving up its liquidity by lending it.
cards.explanation: Demand to borrow the most liquid issue is high, and the holders of that issue must be compensated for lending it, which pushes its repo rate below the general collateral rate.
cards.originalText: Most Treasury shorts are held briefly and prefer the most liquid issue so they can be covered quickly and cheaply, while holders of that issue require compensation to give up its liquidity by lending it.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: The on-the-run Treasury note trades special because it carries less credit risk than older Treasury issues, so cash lenders accept a lower repo rate to hold it as collateral.
cards.explanation: All Treasury issues carry the same issuer credit. Specialness reflects liquidity and demand to borrow, not credit quality.
cards.originalText: The OTR note carries less credit risk than older Treasury issues, so cash lenders accept a lower repo rate to hold it as collateral.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: Older Treasury issues stop being eligible as repo collateral once a new issue is auctioned, so all demand for Treasury collateral moves to the on-the-run note.
cards.explanation: Older issues remain eligible general collateral. They repo close to the general collateral rate because few participants want to borrow them specifically.
cards.originalText: Older issues stop being eligible as repo collateral once a new issue is auctioned, so all demand for Treasury collateral moves to the OTR note.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: The Treasury restricts how much of each new issue may be lent in repo until the next auction, which creates an artificial scarcity of the on-the-run note.
cards.explanation: There is no such Treasury rule. Lendable supply is limited because some owners choose not to lend for institutional reasons.
cards.originalText: The Treasury restricts how much of each new issue may be lent in repo until the next auction, which creates an artificial scarcity of the OTR note.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: Before May 2009, the special repo rate on a Treasury could not fall below 0%, because borrowing the bond at a 0% repo rate left a short seller no better off than failing to deliver, so the special spread was capped at the general collateral rate.
cards.explanation: A trader who fails to deliver earns no interest on the sale proceeds, and so does a trader who borrows the bond at a 0% repo rate. Before May 2009 there was no other penalty, so the special rate had a floor at zero.
cards.originalText: The special rate could not fall below 0%, because borrowing the bond at a 0% repo rate left a short seller no better off than failing; the spread was therefore capped at the GC rate.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: Before May 2009, the special repo rate on a Treasury could not fall below the general collateral rate, because a short seller who failed to deliver could always lend its cash at the general collateral rate instead.
cards.explanation: A trader who fails to deliver does not receive the sale proceeds, so it cannot lend the cash. The floor was on the special rate at 0%, which capped the special spread at the general collateral rate.
cards.originalText: The special rate could not fall below the GC rate, because a short seller who failed to deliver could always lend its cash at GC instead.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: Since May 2009, the penalty for failing to deliver a Treasury is max(3% minus the fed funds target, 0) per year, so the special repo rate can fall below 0% and the penalty rate, not the general collateral rate, caps the special spread.
cards.explanation: With the fed funds target near zero the penalty is about 3% a year, so borrowing a bond at a slightly negative repo rate is still cheaper than failing. The old cap at the general collateral rate no longer applies.
cards.originalText: Since May 2009 a failing trader pays a penalty of max(3% − fed funds target, 0), about 3% here, so borrowing at −0.10% beats failing; the penalty rate, not GC, now caps the spread.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
cards.statement: The penalty for failing to deliver a Treasury rises with the fed funds target, so it is at its minimum when rates are near zero.
cards.explanation: The penalty is max(3% minus the fed funds target, 0), so it falls as the target rises and is at its maximum of 3% when rates are near zero.
cards.originalText: The penalty for failing rises with the fed funds target, so with rates near zero it was at its minimum and cannot explain a negative special rate.
cards.correction: The penalty for failing to deliver a Treasury falls as the fed funds target rises, so it is at its maximum when rates are near zero.

changes.from: rises with the fed funds target
changes.to: falls as the fed funds target rises

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: European banks faced a U.S. dollar shortage in the crisis because they had built large net long U.S. dollar positions in non-bank assets funded by short-term interbank borrowing, FX swaps and money market fund paper, so their funding shortened just as the assets became harder to sell.
cards.explanation: European banks' long dollar positions were funded in their own currencies and swapped, plus short-term dollar borrowing. When these sources withdrew, funding shortened while the assets were harder to sell.
cards.originalText: They had built large net long US dollar positions in non-bank assets funded by short-term interbank borrowing, FX swaps and money market fund paper, so when those sources withdrew, their funding shortened just as the assets became harder to sell.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: Before the crisis, the major European banking systems had built large net short U.S. dollar positions, borrowing dollars short-term to fund long-term lending in their home currencies.
cards.explanation: The major European banking systems were net long U.S. dollars: dollar assets funded in home currency and swapped. Borrowing dollars to fund home-currency lending describes Spanish banks until mid-2006, which were the exception.
cards.originalText: They had built large net short US dollar positions, borrowing dollars short-term to fund long-term lending in their home currencies, so when dollar lenders withdrew they had no dollar assets left to sell to repay them.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: The U.S. dollar shortage arose only at banks with large losses on U.S. structured finance products, since banks whose dollar assets were mainly Treasury and agency securities could roll over their dollar funding throughout the crisis.
cards.explanation: The shortage was a system-wide funding mismatch. Banks with liquid U.S. government securities still had to roll over the short-term dollar funding behind all of their dollar assets as suppliers withdrew.
cards.originalText: The shortage arose only at banks with large losses on US structured finance products, since banks whose dollar assets were mainly US Treasury and agency securities could roll over their dollar funding throughout the crisis.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: A central bank can supply liquidity without limit in its own currency but cannot create foreign currency, so a foreign currency funding gap can be met only from FX reserves or from international sources.
cards.explanation: In the home currency the central bank can act as lender of last resort, but central banks cannot create foreign currencies. Help with foreign currency needs is limited by FX reserves or must come from international sources.
cards.originalText: A central bank can supply liquidity without limit in its own currency but cannot create foreign currency, so a foreign currency funding gap can be met only from FX reserves or from international sources.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: Maturity transformation is not a normal banking function in foreign currencies, so any foreign currency funding gap breaches prudential rules.
cards.explanation: Maturity transformation is a normal banking function in any currency. The problem with foreign currency gaps is the missing backstop, because central banks cannot create foreign currency.
cards.originalText: Maturity transformation is not a normal banking function in foreign currencies, so any foreign currency funding gap breaches prudential rules.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: A national central bank can act as lender of last resort in any currency in which its banks borrow.
cards.explanation: A national central bank can create only its own currency. It cannot create foreign currency, so it cannot act as an unlimited lender of last resort in foreign currencies.
cards.originalText: A national central bank can act as lender of last resort in any currency its banks borrow in, so foreign currency gaps only need to be reported to it more often.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: Residency-based statistics can show a currency mismatch at a host country's offices of foreign banks that the bank does not have on a consolidated basis, while home-country data can miss mismatches booked by the banks' offices abroad.
cards.explanation: Large banks manage positions globally, so a mismatch at one office can be offset elsewhere in the group. Only consolidated data reveal the true position.
cards.originalText: A dollar mismatch booked by a foreign bank’s London oﬀice can be offset elsewhere in its group, so UK data can show a mismatch the bank does not have, while home-country data can miss mismatches its banks book abroad.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: Residency-based statistics adequately capture banks' mismatches, because large banks manage currency and maturity positions office by office, so each host country's statistics reflect the offices located there.
cards.explanation: Large banks manage currency and maturity positions on a consolidated global basis, not office by office, so residency-based data can mislead.
cards.originalText: Residency data are adequate, because large banks manage currency and maturity positions oﬀice by oﬀice, so each host country’s statistics capture the mismatches of the oﬀices located there.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: Residency-based data miss little for Swiss banks, because the great majority of Swiss banks' foreign claims are booked by their offices in Switzerland.
cards.explanation: Only about 18% of Swiss banks' foreign claims are booked in Switzerland, so residency data miss most of the book.
cards.originalText: Residency data miss little for Swiss banks, because the great majority of Swiss banks’ foreign claims are booked by their oﬀices in Switzerland.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: During the global financial crisis, European central banks could not create U.S. dollars and their FX reserves were far below their banks' dollar funding gap, so the dollars had to come from the Federal Reserve through the central banks that supervise the banks.
cards.explanation: Home central banks can address pressures in their own currencies but cannot create dollars, and reserves covered only a fraction of the gap. The Fed could supply the dollars through swap lines.
cards.originalText: Home central banks cannot create dollars, and their FX reserves of about USD 294 billion were far below the dollar funding gap, so the dollars had to come from the Fed through the central banks that supervise the banks.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: During the global financial crisis, euro area, Swiss and UK central banks held more than enough dollar reserves to cover their banks' dollar needs, but swap lines were cheaper than selling reserves.
cards.explanation: Their FX reserves were far smaller than the banks' dollar funding gap, an order of magnitude smaller in the paper's words, so the dollars had to come from the Federal Reserve.
cards.originalText: Euro area, Swiss and UK central banks held more than enough dollar reserves to cover their banks’ needs, but swap lines were cheaper than selling reserves.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: The Federal Reserve's swap lines allowed it to lend directly to European commercial banks, which otherwise had no access to dollars.
cards.explanation: The Fed lent to foreign central banks, which then on-lent the dollars to commercial banks in their jurisdictions. European banks with U.S. offices could already use Fed facilities.
cards.originalText: Swap lines allowed the Fed to lend directly to European commercial banks, which otherwise had no access to dollars.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: Usage of the Federal Reserve's dollar swap lines peaked at about USD 583 billion in December 2008 and fell to about USD 50 billion by early October 2009 as Libor levels and spreads receded, although reliance on public dollar funding may have delayed balance sheet restructuring.
cards.explanation: Falling usage reflected normalizing markets rather than failure. The caveat is that reliance on official dollar funding may have delayed banks' balance sheet adjustment.
cards.originalText: Usage peaked at about USD 583 billion in December 2008 and fell to about USD 50 billion by early October 2009 as Libor levels and spreads receded, although reliance on public dollar funding may have delayed balance sheet restructuring.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: Usage of the Federal Reserve's swap lines kept rising through 2009 as the crisis spread, which shows that the facility failed to stabilize dollar funding markets.
cards.explanation: Usage fell after December 2008. Falling usage reflected normalizing markets, not failure of the facility.
cards.originalText: Usage of the swap lines kept rising through 2009 as the crisis spread, which shows that the facility failed to stabilise dollar funding markets.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
cards.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
cards.statement: The Federal Reserve's swap lines eliminated European banks' U.S. dollar funding gap by the end of 2008, so no balance sheet adjustment by the banks was needed.
cards.explanation: The gap remained large in 2009, and the concern is precisely that reliance on public dollar funding may have delayed balance sheet adjustment.
cards.originalText: The swap lines eliminated European banks’ US dollar funding gap by the end of 2008, so no balance sheet adjustment by the banks was needed.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A zero cumulative interest-sensitive gap does not make net interest income immune to interest rate changes, because liabilities that reprice earlier in the period than assets raise interest cost before interest income when rates rise.
cards.explanation: The cumulative gap counts only whether items reprice within the period, not when. Daily-repricing liabilities funding assets that reset once a year hurt net interest income when rates rise early in the year.
cards.originalText: The claim is incorrect: the borrowings reprice daily while the loans reset only in December, so a rise in rates early in the year raises interest cost months before it raises loan income, and NII falls.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: With equal volumes of interest-sensitive assets and liabilities in the planning period, interest revenue and interest cost change by the same amount whatever the path of rates.
cards.explanation: Equal volumes in the period do not mean equal timing of repricing. If liabilities reprice sooner than assets, a rate move changes cost before it changes income.
cards.originalText: The claim is correct: with equal volumes of interest-sensitive assets and liabilities in the planning period, interest revenue and interest cost change by the same amount whatever the path of rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A zero interest-sensitive gap implies a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap, so net interest income falls whenever rates rise.
cards.explanation: The interest-sensitive gap and the duration gap measure different things, the first relating to net interest income and the second to the market value of equity, and neither implies the other.
cards.originalText: The claim is incorrect: a zero interest-sensitive gap implies a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap, so net interest income falls whenever rates rise.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Duration equals calendar maturity only for instruments such as zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills; for instruments that pay out gradually, duration is always less than maturity.
cards.explanation: Interest and principal paid along the way pull the weighted-average time of cash flows forward. The more frequent the payments, the shorter the duration relative to maturity.
cards.originalText: Duration equals calendar maturity only for instruments such as zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills; for instruments that pay out gradually, duration is always less than maturity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: For any loan or security that pays out gradually over time, duration equals calendar maturity, so matching maturities matches durations.
cards.explanation: For instruments that pay gradually, duration is less than maturity, so matching maturities does not match durations.
cards.originalText: For any loan or security that pays out gradually over time, duration equals calendar maturity, so matching maturities matches durations.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Expected prepayments lengthen a loan's duration, because principal is received earlier than scheduled.
cards.explanation: Receiving principal earlier shortens duration. Prepayments are a limitation of duration gap management because they make cash flows, and hence duration, uncertain.
cards.originalText: Expected prepayments lengthen a loan’s duration, because principal is received earlier than scheduled.
cards.correction: Expected prepayments shorten a loan's duration, because principal is received earlier than scheduled.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: The longer an instrument's maturity, the closer its duration is to its maturity, so the approximation is most reliable for long-term mortgages.
cards.explanation: The shorter the maturity, the closer duration is to maturity. Long-term mortgages are where the two differ most.
cards.originalText: The longer an instrument’s maturity, the closer its duration is to its maturity, so the approximation is most reliable for long-term mortgages.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: Duration gap management assumes small, parallel shifts in the yield curve, so a large move in which short and long rates change by different amounts undermines the hedge, and durations themselves drift as rates change.
cards.explanation: A zero leverage-adjusted duration gap offsets asset and liability value changes only for a small, parallel change in rates, because duration is a linear approximation.
cards.originalText: Duration gap management assumes small, parallel shifts in the yield curve; a large move in which short and long rates change by different amounts violates both assumptions, and durations themselves drift as rates change.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.topic: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
cards.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
cards.statement: A zero leverage-adjusted duration gap protects a bank's net worth against any change in interest rates.
cards.explanation: A zero leverage-adjusted gap protects net worth only against small, parallel shifts in rates. Large or non-parallel moves, and drifting durations, can still change net worth.
cards.originalText: A zero leverage-adjusted duration gap protects net worth against any change in rates, so the loss must have come from the bank’s interest-sensitive gap.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: Northern Rock's liquidity failure came from funding long-term mortgage lending with short-term wholesale debt and securitization, leaving it with no fallback when investors stopped lending in 2007.
cards.explanation: The failure was a funding mismatch between long-term assets and short-term wholesale and securitization funding that disappeared in stress. The retail run followed news of its emergency borrowing from the Bank of England.
cards.originalText: It funded long‑term mortgage lending with short‑term wholesale debt and relied on securitization, so it had no fallback when investors stopped lending in 2007.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: Northern Rock relied mainly on retail deposits, and a retail run began before wholesale markets closed.
cards.explanation: Its root problem was short-term wholesale funding that could not be rolled over. The retail run followed the public report of its emergency borrowing from the Bank of England.
cards.originalText: It relied mainly on retail deposits, which are the least stable source of funding, and a retail run began before wholesale markets closed.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: The case of Metallgesellschaft in 1993 illustrates that hedging long-term liabilities by rolling forward short-term futures contracts may create cash flow mismatches.
cards.explanation: The futures were marked to market daily and generated immediate margin calls when oil prices fell, while the offsetting gains on the long-dated fixed-price contracts would be realized only years later.
cards.originalText: Hedging liabilities by rolling forward short‑term futures contracts may create cash flow mismatches.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: A lack of confidence can contribute to an institution's liquidity funding problems.
cards.explanation: Confidence drives deposit and wholesale funding. When it is lost, depositors withdraw and lenders refuse to roll funding, even for a solvent firm.
cards.originalText: A lack of confidence can contribute to an institution’s liquidity funding problems.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: Wholesale deposits are the most stable source of funding for a financial institution.
cards.explanation: Wholesale deposits are a more volatile source of funding than retail deposits and can disappear quickly in stress.
cards.originalText: Wholesale deposits are the most stable source of funding.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: A solvent firm cannot experience a liquidity funding problem; only an insolvent firm can.
cards.explanation: Liquidity and solvency are different. A solvent firm can fail from funding problems, as Northern Rock did, when it cannot raise cash to meet its obligations.
cards.originalText: A solvent firm cannot experience a liquidity funding problem; only an insolvent firm can.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: Stressed markets can limit the effectiveness of trading book liquidation as a source of liquidity.
cards.explanation: Liquidating the trading book raises cash only if the book is liquid. In stress, bid-ask spreads widen and buyers vanish, so liquidation works poorly exactly when it is needed.
cards.originalText: Stressed markets can limit the effectiveness of trading book liquidation strategies.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: Investments in Treasury securities help a bank increase its risk and return profile.
cards.explanation: Treasuries offer liquidity at a low return, so they reduce rather than increase a bank's risk and return profile.
cards.originalText: Investments in Treasury securities help a bank increase its risk and return profile.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
cards.statement: Central bank borrowings are a relatively cheap way for banks to stay afloat.
cards.explanation: Central bank borrowing is costly: it carries a high interest rate and a collateral haircut, and it sends a negative signal to the market.
cards.originalText: Central bank borrowings are relatively cheap ways for banks to stay afloat.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Selling automatically when an asset's price falls below a pre-set stop-loss level is an example of positive feedback trading.
cards.explanation: A stop-loss rule forces selling after prices fall, which pushes prices lower and triggers further sales. This amplifies trends and drains liquidity.
cards.originalText: A trader sells automatically when an asset’s price falls below a pre‑set stop‑loss level.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A fund that rebalances to its target weights by buying an equity whose price has fallen is engaging in positive feedback trading.
cards.explanation: Buying after a price fall trades against the move, which is negative feedback trading and stabilizes prices.
cards.originalText: A fund rebalances to its target weights by buying an equity whose price has fallen.
cards.correction: A fund that rebalances to its target weights by buying an equity whose price has fallen is engaging in negative feedback trading.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A holder of a long option position who delta-hedges by selling the underlying after a price increase is engaging in positive feedback trading.
cards.explanation: Delta-hedging a long option position sells after price rises and buys after falls, which is negative feedback. It is the dynamic hedging of short option positions that is positive feedback.
cards.originalText: A holder of a long option position delta‑hedges by selling the underlying after a price increase.
cards.correction: A holder of a long option position who delta-hedges by selling the underlying after a price increase is engaging in negative feedback trading.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Negative feedback traders, who trade against price moves, supply counterparties on both sides and contribute to a stable, liquid market.
cards.explanation: A liquid market has a balance of buyers and sellers dominated by negative feedback traders, who buy on declines and sell on rises.
cards.originalText: Negative feedback traders

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Stop-loss rules contribute to a stable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Stop-loss rules force sales into falling markets, which is positive feedback that drains liquidity.
cards.originalText: Stop loss rules

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Trend trading contributes to a stable market with respect to liquidity.
cards.explanation: Trend traders follow price direction, which amplifies moves and removes counterparties, so trend trading is a positive feedback behavior that undermines liquidity.
cards.originalText: Trend trading

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A majority of large investors increasingly following a trend-following trading strategy is a warning sign of a potential liquidity black hole.
cards.explanation: Widespread trend following is positive feedback trading: investors all sell into declines, so buyers vanish as prices fall and a liquidity black hole can develop.
cards.originalText: A majority of large investors increasingly follow a trend‑following trading strategy.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Portfolio managers selling stocks that have increased in value and reached their price target is a warning sign of a potential liquidity black hole.
cards.explanation: Selling into strength is negative feedback trading, which supplies counterparties and supports liquidity.
cards.originalText: Portfolio managers sell stocks that have increased in value and reached their price target.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: Narrower bid-ask spreads for less liquid stocks are a warning sign of a potential liquidity black hole.
cards.explanation: Narrower spreads indicate better, not worse, liquidity.
cards.originalText: Bid‑ask spreads for less liquid stocks become narrower.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A highly liquid market tends to result when negative feedback traders sell shares as prices rise.
cards.explanation: Negative feedback traders sell into rises and buy into falls, providing counterparties on both sides and keeping prices stable.
cards.originalText: negative feedback traders sell shares as prices rise.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A highly liquid market tends to result from stop-loss rules taking effect as prices decline.
cards.explanation: Stop-loss selling as prices fall amplifies the decline and reduces liquidity.
cards.originalText: stop‑loss rules take effect as prices decline.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
cards.statement: A highly liquid market tends to result when positive feedback traders purchase shares as prices rise.
cards.explanation: Buying as prices rise is positive feedback trading, which pushes prices further in the same direction and reduces stability and liquidity.
cards.originalText: positive feedback traders purchase shares as prices rise.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: A bank that has lost access to intraday credit should delay or throttle its non-critical outgoing payments so that payments are released only up to its cash balances plus the incoming funds it has received.
cards.explanation: Without intraday credit, available funds are limited to opening cash balances plus incoming funds flow. Outgoing payments are the largest use of intraday liquidity, so the bank controls their timing, paying critical items first, until receipts rebuild its balance.
cards.originalText: Delay or throttle non‑critical outgoing payments so that payments are released only up to cash balances plus incoming funds received.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: A bank that loses access to intraday credit has failed and must declare insolvency, because its obligations can no longer be met.
cards.explanation: Losing one source of intraday liquidity does not by itself mean failure. The bank can manage the constraint by controlling the timing of its outgoing payments until incoming receipts arrive.
cards.originalText: Declare insolvency, because loss of intraday credit means obligations cannot be met.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: A bank can take no action on an intraday shortfall until the end-of-day PCS settlement, because intraday shortfalls are resolved at that point.
cards.explanation: PCS settlement happens once, near the end of the day, so waiting would leave payments unmade throughout the day. A bank must manage its intraday position actively, for example by timing its outgoing payments.
cards.originalText: Take no action until the end‑of‑day PCS settlement, because intraday shortfalls are resolved at that point.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Funding of nostro accounts, meaning a cash transfer to a correspondent bank as compensation for its services, is a use of intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Banks fund correspondent (nostro) accounts abroad to compensate the correspondent for services such as foreign transactions. Such a transfer is a use of intraday liquidity.
cards.originalText: Funding of nostro accounts.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Settlements at payment, clearing and settlement (PCS) systems typically occur once a day, mainly in the late afternoon, and can be either a source or a use of intraday liquidity depending on the participant's net position.
cards.explanation: PCS settlement is a net, once-a-day, late-afternoon settlement, so it is a source for a net receiver and a use for a net payer. It is easier to forecast for multi-day settlements than for same-day settlement activity.
cards.originalText: Settlements at payment, clearing and settlement (PCS) systems.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Overnight borrowings, such as federal funds borrowed in the afternoon and returned the next morning, are a source of intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Funds borrowed in the interbank market and repaid the following morning are overnight borrowings. They differ from intraday credit because they are repaid only the next day, and they supply cash to the bank during the day.
cards.originalText: Overnight borrowings; funding of nostro accounts.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Funding of nostro accounts at a correspondent bank outside the home market is a use of intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Funding nostro accounts is a cash outflow to correspondent banks. The uses of intraday liquidity are outgoing wires, PCS settlements, nostro funding, collateral pledging and asset purchases or funding.
cards.originalText: Funding of nostro accounts at a correspondent bank outside the home market.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Incoming funds flow is a use of intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Incoming funds flow is the largest source of intraday liquidity, not a use.
cards.originalText: Incoming funds flow.
cards.correction: Incoming funds flow is a source of intraday liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Entering a term repo as the repo seller is a use of intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Selling securities through a term repo raises cash, so it is other term funding, which is a source of intraday liquidity.
cards.originalText: Term repo (as the repo seller).
cards.correction: Entering a term repo as the repo seller is a source of intraday liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Intraday credit is a use of intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Intraday credit, such as a central bank line of credit or net debit cap, is a source of intraday liquidity.
cards.originalText: Intraday credit (e.g., Federal Reserve unsecured committed line of credit).
cards.correction: Intraday credit is a source of intraday liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Immediately selling long-term illiquid assets at market prices is an effective way to raise cash for same-day transactions during an intraday liquidity crunch.
cards.explanation: Illiquid assets cannot be converted reliably into same-day cash, and a fire sale is costly and signals distress. Controlling outgoing payments, borrowing overnight funds and obtaining intraday credit are the effective same-day tools.
cards.originalText: Sell long‑term illiquid assets immediately at market prices to raise cash for same‑day transactions.
cards.correction: Immediately selling long-term illiquid assets at market prices is not an effective way to raise cash for same-day transactions during an intraday liquidity crunch.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Prioritising critical payments and delaying non-essential outgoing transfers while monitoring liquidity in real time helps mitigate intraday liquidity stress.
cards.explanation: Outgoing payments are a large use of intraday liquidity and can be delayed until incoming receipts arrive, so controlling their timing eases the stress.
cards.originalText: Prioritise critical payments and delay non‑essential outgoing transfers while monitoring liquidity in real time.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Borrowing federal funds or other overnight funding in the interbank market and returning it the next morning is a way to cover an intraday liquidity shortfall.
cards.explanation: Overnight borrowings are a source of intraday funds. They are repaid the next morning, so they can bridge a same-day shortfall.
cards.originalText: Borrow federal funds or other overnight funding in the interbank market to cover the shortfall, returning it the next morning.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Requesting intraday credit from the central bank or from correspondent banks is a standard way to bridge a temporary intraday liquidity shortfall.
cards.explanation: Intraday credit is a standard source of intraday liquidity that allows temporary overdrafts to be covered.
cards.originalText: Request intraday credit from the central bank or correspondent banks to bridge the shortfall.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: A bank's clients can be a source of intraday liquidity, because the bank can convert liquid assets such as US Treasury bills into cash through transactions with them, for example a repo.
cards.explanation: A repo with a client turns Treasury bills into same-day cash, so clients can supply intraday liquidity to the bank.
cards.originalText: The bank’s clients can serve as a source of intraday liquidity, which allows the bank to convert liquid assets such as US Treasury bills to cash.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: US regulators prohibit banks from running intraday overdrafts.
cards.explanation: Intraday credit and daylight overdrafts are permitted in the United States. The Federal Reserve provides intraday credit within a net debit cap and charges interest on it.
cards.originalText: Intraday overdrafts are prohibited by regulators, but the bank can borrow from the Federal Reserve before the opening of business to resolve expected liquidity needs.
cards.correction: US regulators permit banks to run intraday overdrafts.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: The balance of money market assets in a bank's investment portfolio tends to be volatile and is therefore difficult to forecast on any given day.
cards.explanation: Liquid asset balances, including money market assets, have low volatility and are predictable.
cards.originalText: The balance of money market assets in the bank’s investment portfolio tends to be volatile and is therefore difficult to forecast on any given day.
cards.correction: The balance of money market assets in a bank's investment portfolio tends to have low volatility and is therefore easy to forecast on any given day.

changes.from: tends to be volatile and is therefore difficult to forecast
changes.to: tends to have low volatility and is therefore easy to forecast

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Funding of nostro accounts at correspondent banks is typically initiated by clients entering into loans or repo transactions.
cards.explanation: Nostro funding is initiated by the bank itself, not directly by its clients.
cards.originalText: Funding of nostro accounts at correspondent banks is typically initiated by clients entering into loans or repo transactions.
cards.correction: Funding of nostro accounts at correspondent banks is typically initiated by the bank itself rather than by clients entering into loans or repo transactions.

changes.to: initiated by the bank itself rather than by clients

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Pledging collateral is a use of intraday liquidity that can create an intraday overdraft, which a bank can cover with intraday credit from the central bank.
cards.explanation: Pledging collateral is a cash outflow that can overdraw an account, and intraday central bank credit is a standard source for covering the overdraft.
cards.originalText: The bank pledges cash collateral against a purchase of OTC securities, which leads it to borrow intraday funds from the US Federal Reserve to eliminate the overdraft.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Incoming funds from customers are a cause of an intraday overdraft at a bank.
cards.explanation: Incoming customer funds are a source of intraday liquidity, so they reduce an overdraft rather than cause one. Overdrafts are caused by outflows such as wires, settlements and collateral pledging.
cards.originalText: Customers transfer funds to the bank in advance of an expected purchase of real estate, which leads the bank to deposit funds into a special account to eliminate the overdraft.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: An increase in a bank's net debit cap triggers an intraday overdraft.
cards.explanation: A higher net debit cap only permits a larger overdraft; it does not cause one. Overdrafts arise from outgoing payments that exceed available funds.
cards.originalText: The FMU increases the bank’s net debit cap, which triggers an overdraft and leads the bank to initiate a reverse repurchase agreement to provide the necessary intraday liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Outgoing wire transfers are the most significant use of intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Outgoing wires, made for the bank itself or for its clients, are the largest and most continuous outflow, paid throughout the day and managed against the intraday credit limit.
cards.originalText: Outgoing wire transfers.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Among sources of intraday liquidity, intraday credit is likely to have the greatest explicit financial cost, because the central bank may charge interest or require collateral.
cards.explanation: Cash balances and liquid assets are owned, so they carry only an implicit opportunity cost, and incoming funds flow has no explicit cost. Intraday credit is borrowed and may carry interest or collateral requirements.
cards.originalText: Intraday credit.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Cash flow volatility increases a bank treasurer's challenge in managing cash to stay within intraday credit limits.
cards.explanation: Sudden inflows and outflows make the intraday overdraft hard to control, so volatile cash flows are a key challenge.
cards.originalText: Cash flow volatility.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Insufficient real-time data increases a bank treasurer's challenge in managing cash to stay within intraday credit limits.
cards.explanation: Without real-time balances the treasurer cannot see current cash or remaining needs, which makes staying within credit limits harder.
cards.originalText: Insufficient real‑time data.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.statement: Securities price volatility increases a bank treasurer's challenge in managing cash to stay within intraday credit limits.
cards.explanation: Price moves trigger margin calls and collateral outflows, which add to intraday cash needs and make credit limits harder to respect.
cards.originalText: Securities price volatility.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Time-sensitive obligations are a measure for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.
cards.explanation: Time-sensitive obligations, such as margin calls that must settle at a specific time, are a measure for understanding intraday flows. The risk-level measures are daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital, client intraday credit usage and payment throughput.
cards.originalText: Time‑sensitive obligations
cards.correction: Time-sensitive obligations are a measure for understanding intraday flows.

changes.from: quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Client intraday credit usage is a measure for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.
cards.explanation: It compares a client's peak daily intraday overdraft with its credit line, and is one of the four risk-level measures.
cards.originalText: Client intraday credit usage

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital is a measure for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.
cards.explanation: It compares the unsecured, available intraday credit with Tier 1 capital, and serves as a proxy for systemic risk.
cards.originalText: Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage and client intraday credit usage are both measures for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.
cards.explanation: The risk-level measures are daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital, client intraday credit usage and payment throughput. Credit-line totals and time-sensitive obligations are flow-tracking measures.
cards.originalText: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage and client intraday credit usage

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: For each payment, a bank stores the counterparty's long-term credit rating as part of its payment-level data on total payments.
cards.explanation: Per-payment records describe the payment and its processing: amount, times, routing, payer and payee, payment system and any suspensions. A counterparty's credit rating is not a payment attribute.
cards.originalText: The counterparty’s long‑term credit rating

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: For each payment, a bank stores the payment amount and the time at which it was received or originated.
cards.explanation: Amount and timing are core payment-level data held in the total payments record used to understand intraday flows.
cards.originalText: Payment amount and time received or originated

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: For each payment, a bank stores the routing information and the payment system used.
cards.explanation: Routing information and payment system are part of the per-payment record stored under the total payments measure.
cards.originalText: Routing information and payment system used

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: For each payment, a bank stores the payer and the payee.
cards.explanation: The identity of payer and payee is part of the per-payment record stored under the total payments measure.
cards.originalText: Payer and payee

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Payment-level records such as payer and payee, payment system used, suspensions, time received or originated and routing information fall under the total payments measure for understanding intraday flows.
cards.explanation: These per-payment details define the total payments measure. They allow summaries such as payments sent and received by client type and the net settlement-account position through the day.
cards.originalText: Total payments

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Client intraday credit usage is derived by comparing a client's peak daily intraday overdraft with its established credit line.
cards.explanation: Aggregated across clients, it shows how much liquidity the bank needs to support client activity.
cards.originalText: Client intraday credit usage

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Payment throughput is derived by comparing a client's peak daily intraday overdraft with its established credit line.
cards.explanation: Payment throughput measures outgoing payments as a proportion of total payments over the day. Comparing a client's peak overdraft with its credit line gives client intraday credit usage.
cards.originalText: Payment throughput
cards.correction: Client intraday credit usage is derived by comparing a client's peak daily intraday overdraft with its established credit line.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage is derived by comparing a client's peak daily intraday overdraft with its established credit line.
cards.explanation: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage uses the bank's own largest net negative balance relative to its credit line, not a client's.
cards.originalText: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage
cards.correction: Client intraday credit usage is derived by comparing a client's peak daily intraday overdraft with its established credit line.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Tracking intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility, with as much transaction-level detail as possible and snapshots of account and collateral positions at securities settlement networks, describes the other cash transactions measure for understanding intraday flows.
cards.explanation: Other cash transactions covers position tracking at all FMUs plus account and collateral snapshots at securities settlement networks. It is distinct from total payments, which is payment-level data on electronic payments.
cards.originalText: Other cash transactions

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Other cash transactions, covering FMU position and collateral tracking, is a measure for understanding intraday flows.
cards.explanation: Other cash transactions is a flow-tracking measure. The risk-level measures are daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital, client intraday credit usage and payment throughput.
cards.originalText: Other cash transactions

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital is a measure for understanding intraday flows.
cards.explanation: It is a risk-level measure that compares unsecured, available intraday credit with Tier 1 capital and acts as a systemic risk indicator.
cards.originalText: Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital
cards.correction: Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital is a measure for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.

changes.to: quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage is a measure for understanding intraday flows.
cards.explanation: It is a risk-level measure: the bank's largest negative balance during the day relative to its credit line.
cards.originalText: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage
cards.correction: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage is a measure for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.

changes.to: quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Payment throughput is a measure for understanding intraday flows.
cards.explanation: Payment throughput, the share of outgoing payments made by time of day, is a risk-level measure although it is easily confused with payment flow data.
cards.originalText: Payment throughput
cards.correction: Payment throughput is a measure for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.

changes.to: quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: A bank measures payment throughput in order to determine the best means of acquiring intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Payment throughput is tracked for three reasons: timely processing, compliance with FMU target-percentage requirements, and identifying peak periods and their link to liquidity and credit usage. Choosing a funding source is not one of them.
cards.originalText: To determine the best means of acquiring intraday liquidity

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: A bank measures payment throughput to track volume patterns and help ensure that all of the day's payments are processed on time.
cards.explanation: Timely processing is the first of the reasons for tracking outgoing payments relative to total payments or time markers.
cards.originalText: To track volume patterns and help ensure that all of the day’s payments are processed on time

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: A bank that is a direct participant in an FMU measures payment throughput to meet FMU requirements to submit a target percentage of payments by a deadline.
cards.explanation: Some FMUs require a minimum share of payments to be submitted by set times, and payment throughput shows whether this is being met.
cards.originalText: To meet FMU requirements for submitting a target percentage of payments by a deadline

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: A bank measures payment throughput to identify peak periods over time and their correlation with intraday liquidity on hand and intraday credit usage.
cards.explanation: Linking peak payment periods to liquidity on hand and credit usage is one of the three reasons for monitoring payment throughput.
cards.originalText: To identify peak periods over time and their correlation with intraday liquidity on hand and intraday credit usage

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Total payments is a measure for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels.
cards.explanation: Total payments is a flow-tracking measure covering payment amounts, timing and net settlement-account position. The risk-level measures are daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital, client intraday credit usage and payment throughput.
cards.originalText: Total payments
cards.correction: Total payments is a measure for understanding intraday flows.

changes.from: quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Payment throughput, the proportion of outgoing payments made and when they occur during the day, is the risk-level metric that helps a bank confirm that it meets an FMU's requirement to settle a minimum share of payments by set times.
cards.explanation: Payment throughput monitors payment patterns and shows whether outgoing payments are being sent on time, which directly addresses FMU timing requirements.
cards.originalText: Payment throughput, the proportion of outgoing payments made and when they occur during the day.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, the largest net cumulative negative position during the day relative to the credit line, is an appropriate indicator for monitoring intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: Intraday risk arises from the path of balances during the day, so the indicator must capture the intraday extreme. This measure shows the peak funding need.
cards.originalText: The bank’s daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, measured as the largest net cumulative negative position during the day relative to the credit line.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: A bank's end-of-day net settlement position across all payment systems is an appropriate indicator for monitoring its intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: The end-of-day net position can be flat even if the bank was deeply overdrawn during the day, so it hides intraday exposure.
cards.originalText: The bank’s end‑of‑day net settlement position across all payment systems.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: A bank's liquidity coverage ratio calculated at the close of each business day is an appropriate indicator for monitoring its intraday liquidity.
cards.explanation: The LCR is a 30-day stress measure calculated at a point in time, so it does not capture intraday peaks in liquidity usage.
cards.originalText: The bank’s liquidity coverage ratio calculated at the close of each business day.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
cards.statement: Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital, the ratio of unsecured and available intraday credit to Tier 1 capital, is the metric that gauges a bank's intraday settlement risk and the systemic risk it contributes.
cards.explanation: It shows how large the bank's intraday settlement exposure is relative to its loss-absorbing capital.
cards.originalText: Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: In monitoring liquidity, cash flows are classified along the two dimensions of time and amount, each of which can be deterministic or stochastic.
cards.explanation: A cash flow is characterised by when it occurs and how large it is, and in each dimension it is either known (deterministic) or random (stochastic).
cards.originalText: Group A

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: In monitoring liquidity, cash flows are classified along the two dimensions of time and credit scores.
cards.explanation: The two dimensions are time and amount. Credit is only one possible source of uncertainty in the amount of a cash flow.
cards.originalText: Group B
cards.correction: In monitoring liquidity, cash flows are classified along the two dimensions of time and amount.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: In monitoring liquidity, cash flows are classified along the two dimensions of term structure and time.
cards.explanation: The two dimensions are time and amount. Term structure describes a maturity profile, not a classification dimension of cash flows.
cards.originalText: Group D
cards.correction: In monitoring liquidity, cash flows are classified along the two dimensions of time and amount.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: Deterministic cash flows occur at predictable future instants and in an amount known with certainty.
cards.explanation: A cash flow is deterministic only when both its timing and its amount are known in advance.
cards.originalText: They occur at predictable future instants and in an amount known with certainty.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: Deterministic cash flows occur at random future instants, and their amount cannot be fully determined.
cards.explanation: Cash flows that are random in timing and amount are stochastic. Deterministic cash flows have both timing and amount known with certainty.
cards.originalText: They occur at random future instants, and their amount cannot be fully determined.
cards.correction: Stochastic cash flows occur at random future instants, and their amount cannot be fully determined.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: Deterministic cash flows have an amount that cannot be predicted but occur at predictable future instants.
cards.explanation: Known timing with an unknown amount, as with a floating-rate coupon, is stochastic in amount. A deterministic cash flow has both timing and amount known with certainty.
cards.originalText: Their amount cannot be predicted, but they occur at predictable future instants.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: Contractual cash flows on fixed-rate bonds, fixed-rate mortgages and loans, and on bonds issued or loans received by the bank, arising from periodic interest and capital repayments, are deterministic cash flows.
cards.explanation: Fixed-rate contractual schedules fix both the dates and the amounts in advance, which is the definition of deterministic cash flows.
cards.originalText: Deterministic cash flows

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: Cash flows from new debt issued by a bank are stochastic in both timing and amount.
cards.explanation: New debt issuance is scheduled, so its timing is deterministic even though the amount is stochastic.
cards.originalText: new debt issued by a bank.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: A bank's recovery on a client default is a cash flow that is stochastic in both timing and amount.
cards.explanation: Both the date and the size of a recovery are uncertain.
cards.originalText: a bank’s recovery on a client default.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: The payout of an American-style call option is a cash flow that is stochastic in both timing and amount.
cards.explanation: American-style exercise can occur at any time and the payoff depends on the market.
cards.originalText: the payout of an American‑style call option.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
cards.statement: Mortgage prepayments caused by interest rate declines are cash flows that are stochastic in both timing and amount.
cards.explanation: The timing and size of prepayments depend on interest rates and on borrower behaviour.
cards.originalText: mortgage prepayments due to interest rate declines.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
cards.statement: When a customer exercises a liquidity option such as a credit line or a demand deposit, the bank experiences two primary effects: an impact on its balance sheet from the amount repaid or withdrawn, and a positive or negative financial impact.
cards.explanation: Exercise moves cash to or from the bank, changing the balance sheet by that amount. It also creates a gain or loss from the difference between the original contract terms and current market terms.
cards.originalText: An impact on the balance sheet from the amount repaid or withdrawn, and a (positive or negative) financial impact.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
cards.statement: Liquidity options may or may not be financially profitable upon exercise, because they are exercised to meet a liquidity need.
cards.explanation: Unlike standard financial options, which are exercised when profitable, liquidity options are exercised because the holder needs or wants to supply liquidity, so exercise is not tied to profitability.
cards.originalText: Liquidity options may or may not be financially profitable upon exercise.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
cards.statement: Liquidity options are exercised only when exercise is financially profitable to the holder.
cards.explanation: That rule applies to standard financial options. Liquidity options are exercised to meet a liquidity need, even when exercise is not profitable.
cards.originalText: Liquidity options are exercised only when exercise is financially profitable to the holder.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
